chunks.title: Apps & tools > Overview
chunks.text:
Ryoku ships a curated toolkit, not a grab bag of everything in the
repositories. The installer lets you keep or leave out most of it (see
Install Ryoku); whatever you leave out stays out after
updates. Want more software? Ryostore adds whole bundles in one click.

chunks.title: Apps & tools > The desktop music player
chunks.text:
The desktop Music player widget follows whichever MPRIS player is active
(Ryotunes, Spotify, a browser tab or `mpv`), with artwork, transport and a
seekbar.

For Spotify, its backdrop can play the track's Spotify Canvas. The Canvas
token is only readable inside the Spotify client, so `ryoku doctor` installs
`spicetify-cli` and wires the bundled `ryoku-canvas` extension for you. The
setup is inert if you do not run Spotify.

chunks.title: Apps & tools > The file manager
chunks.text:
The installer asks for a file manager:

- Files (Nautilus) is recommended: Ryoku's stash actions live in its
  right-click menu.
- Dolphin, KDE's file manager.
- Thunar, Xfce's light file manager.

The one you pick becomes the files role (`Mod + E` and every "open folder"
action) and the default for folders. Change it later in Ryoku Settings >
Keybinds.

chunks.title: Apps & tools > The launcher
chunks.text:
Press `Mod + Space` to open the launcher. Start typing to search apps, open
windows, the web and quick math at once, or lead with a prefix to talk to one
provider directly. `F1` inside the launcher shows this list.

Prefix | What it does
_(none)_ | Apps, open windows, web results and quick math
`/` | Actions: lock, screenshot, media, settings
`/file`, `/folder`, `/image`, `/video` | Find files
`>` | Packages: `>install`, `>remove`, `>search`
`=` | Calculator
`?` | Web search, with `!bang` shortcuts
`@` | Live radio: `@lofi` tunes in, `@stop` tunes out
`\` | One question to the [Rashin](/docs/rashin) agent

The `\` lane needs Rashin; see Rashin.

chunks.title: Apps & tools > The Ryoku apps
chunks.text:
Three of Ryoku's own apps are on by default and listed first in the installer.
Each can be left out there, or removed later; the doctor never puts a removed
app back.

- Ryotunes is the music app. The now-playing widgets and the media keys
  follow it like any other player. It updates from its own releases.
- Ryoport is the dashboard for virtual machines, SSH hosts and serial
  consoles. It ships inside the desktop package, so leaving it out in the
  installer hides its launcher entry instead of removing files.
- RyoManager is the system monitor and task manager: performance graphs
  and the running processes, which you can inspect and end. It reaches
  existing installs once through the doctor.

chunks.title: The ryoku command > Config lay-down: `ryoku materialize`
chunks.text:
`ryoku materialize` lays Ryoku's base config into `~/.config` and then overlays
your edits from `~/.config/ryoku/user_edits`, so a file there wins at its
mirrored path. It clobbers the previous Ryoku copy, prunes files a past release
shipped but this one dropped, and never touches files Ryoku never shipped. The
generated display and GPU drop-ins are seeded only when absent. `ryoku update`
and the installer run it for you; on a source checkout use the deploy instead.

chunks.title: The ryoku command > Emergency: `ryoku recovery`
chunks.text:
The last resort when the desktop is too broken to update normally. It always
restores the stable channel: it pulls `main`, reinstalls the base packages and
redeploys, overwriting Ryoku's configs. It prefers a local copy of
`bin/ryoku-recovery` and otherwise fetches the canonical script, so it still
works when the local build is broken. See Troubleshoot.

chunks.title: The ryoku command > Environment and state
chunks.text:
Variable | What it does
`RYOKU_REPO` | The checkout root, for `deploy` and a source checkout.
`RYOKU_CONFIG_BASE` | Overrides the `materialize` base dir (default `/usr/share/ryoku/config`).
`RYOKU_AI_KEY` | Your provider key for `doctor --explain`, or write it to `~/.config/ryoku/ai-key`.
`RYOKU_AI_URL` | The API base (default `https://api.groq.com/openai/v1`; for OpenRouter use `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1`).
`RYOKU_AI_MODEL` | The model (Groq default `llama-3.3-70b-versatile`).

State lives under `$XDG_STATE_HOME/ryoku` (default `~/.local/state/ryoku`):

File | What it is
`materialized` | The manifest of Ryoku-owned files, so the next `materialize` can prune cleanly.
`update-log.txt` | Everything the last update's tools printed.
`doctor-report.txt` | The latest diagnostic report.
`repo`, `deployed` | The checkout and commit the last deploy laid down (source checkouts).

chunks.title: The ryoku command > Keep it healthy: `ryoku doctor`
chunks.text:
`ryoku doctor` runs the convergent reconcilers: idempotent checks (and, where it
is safe, fixes) for stateful drift the package and config layers cannot express.
A healthy machine is quiet.

```bash
ryoku doctor            # heal what is safe to heal
ryoku doctor --check    # or -n: show what is wrong, change nothing
ryoku doctor --verbose  # also list the checks that passed
```

`ryoku update` runs `ryoku doctor` for you, so a finding never aborts an
  update. Ryoku Settings shows the same findings as a system check.

The reconcilers live in `ryoku/cli/internal/doctor/` and cover desktop
sessions, channel health, the keyring, compositor config, displays and
backlights, pending package config, orphaned packages, duplicate launcher
entries and more, with host-specific checks on each edition. Each one retires
once every supported install has run it.

chunks.title: The ryoku command > One layout everywhere: `ryoku keyboard`
chunks.text:
A keyboard layout has to land in four places: the window manager, the SDDM
greeter, the console, and the boot image, which is what the disk passphrase
prompt uses. The last one is the trap: the keymap is copied in when the boot
image is built, so editing it later never reaches the passphrase prompt.

Command | What it does
`keyboard status [--json]` | Each layer's layout, and whether the boot image predates the current keymap.
`keyboard detect` | The layout this machine records, and which source said so.
`keyboard apply [layout]` | Write the greeter and console keymap, then rebuild the boot image so the passphrase prompt follows. `--no-boot` skips the rebuild.

With no layout, `apply` pushes the desktop's own layout out, and `doctor`
reports any drift with the exact fix.

chunks.title: The ryoku command > Overview
chunks.text:
`ryoku` is the front door to the whole system. It updates the machine, moves it
between channels, rolls it back, reports its state, reloads the desktop and
repairs stateful drift, all from one Go program (`ryoku/cli/`). It does not
reimplement package management or snapshots: it drives pacman, XBPS or DNF and
snapper, and adds the safety rails around them. Run `ryoku help` for the
built-in usage.

chunks.title: The ryoku command > `ryoku owner ...`
chunks.text:
Answers the question to ask before touching a config file: who writes it, and
where your change belongs so an update does not overwrite it.

```text
$ ryoku owner ~/.config/kitty/kitty.conf
/home/you/.config/kitty/kitty.conf
  class:   ryoku
  writer:  the ryoku-desktop package, through materialize
  advice:  Ryoku ships this and overwrites it on every update. Put your change in ~/.config/kitty/user.conf instead.
  edit:    /home/you/.config/kitty/user.conf
```

`--json` prints the same for a tool, and `--map` prints an ownership summary of
the whole machine.

chunks.title: The ryoku command > `ryoku rollback [id]`
chunks.text:
With no arguments it lists published releases and, where the edition supports
them, local snapshots. `ryoku rollback --to ` moves the Ryoku package
set to a frozen release without a reboot; the distribution base and kernel do
not move. After such a move the boot guard watches the next boots and moves the
Ryoku set back if two boots fail to reach a healthy desktop.

`ryoku rollback ` walks you through a whole-system restore:

Reboot, choose Ryoku Linux > Snapshots > id in the Limine menu, run
    `sudo limine-snapper-restore`, then reboot into the restored system.

The snapshots are under Ryoku snapshots in GRUB (hold Shift or press Esc
    while booting). A snapshot boots read-only; to keep it, run
    `sudo ryoku boot-menu restore` in that boot.

chunks.title: The ryoku command > `ryoku snapshots`, `ryoku reload`, `ryoku reset`
chunks.text:
- `ryoku snapshots` lists the root snapshots on editions that provide them.
- `ryoku reload` restarts the shell and reloads the window manager. Use it after
  a hand edit to config that is already in place.
- `ryoku reset [path]` drops an override from `~/.config/ryoku/user_edits`, so
  that file goes back to the Ryoku default. With no path, and after a confirm,
  it drops them all.

chunks.title: The ryoku command > `ryoku status [--json]`
chunks.text:
A read-only report. It prints the active config base, the installed
`ryoku-desktop` version, what the signed repository offers, and the waiting
distribution packages as `system:`. A source checkout shows the channel, the
deployed commit and how far behind it is. When the channel is still building
or its last build failed, a `build:` line says so. `--json` is the data seam
the Hub and the update island read.

chunks.title: The ryoku command > `ryoku track `
chunks.text:
`stable` follows named releases as signed packages. `unstable` builds the box
from the `unstable-dev` branch and, from then on, `ryoku update` fast-forwards
to the last commit the Testing gate passed. A release tag or an unstable build
name pins that frozen version as packages. `ryoku track stable` returns a box
to packages. The package managers move channels in one transaction and restore
the previous repository if the move fails.

chunks.title: The ryoku command > `ryoku update`
chunks.text:
The full, safe update. Where the edition supports snapshots it is wrapped in a
snapper pre and post pair; an unconfigured snapper never blocks the update, but
a failed step aborts before anything else changes.

On a packaged install it moves the packages Ryoku's signed repository serves,
by name, then lays the refreshed config in with `ryoku materialize`, runs
`ryoku doctor` and reloads the shell. It leaves your distribution's own
upgrade (`sudo pacman -Syu`, `sudo xbps-install -Syu`, `sudo dnf5 upgrade
--refresh`) to you and reports how many of those packages are waiting. On a
source checkout it fast-forwards to the last commit that passed the Testing
gate and redeploys.

chunks.title: The ryoku command > `ryoku update`
chunks.text:
Flag | What it does
`--system` | Also run the distribution upgrade, under the same snapshot pair.
`--wait` | Wait for a channel build or source check that is still running.
`--force` | Update despite a build or check in progress.
`-v`, `--verbose` | Stream the raw output instead of the summary.
`--gui` | Run in the background, driven from the Updates page of Ryoku Settings.

On a terminal the run is a short console: one line per step, a progress bar and
a closing card. Everything the tools print goes to
`~/.local/state/ryoku/update-log.txt`; on failure the card shows the error and
the last lines, and offers the pre-update snapshot. Progress is also published
to `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/ryoku-update.json` for the bar's update island. See
Updates for the model.

chunks.text:
The two lanes, channels, snapshots and rollback.

Logs, `ryoku doctor`, rollback and recovery when something breaks.

The override files `materialize` never touches.

chunks.title: The ryoku command > Sign-in: `ryoku keyring` and `ryoku security-key`
chunks.text:
`ryoku keyring` chooses how the GNOME keyring unlocks your saved passwords at
sign-in. The default, `never-ask`, means no app ever prompts;
`unlock-on-login` keeps the store encrypted and unlocks it with your login
password; `ask` leaves it locked until an app asks. The Lockscreen page in
Ryoku Settings drives the same choice.

`ryoku security-key` enrolls a FIDO2/U2F key and turns it on for `sudo`,
polkit prompts or login, either instead of the password or together with it.

chunks.title: The ryoku command > Two worlds
chunks.text:
Every command behaves with respect to one of two ways Ryoku can live on a
machine.

The desktop is installed from Ryoku's signed repository with pacman, XBPS
    or DNF. `ryoku-desktop` ships the base config under
    `/usr/share/ryoku/config`; there is no git checkout and no build toolchain.
    This is what the ISOs and the script installer give you.

The desktop is built from a checkout of the repository and laid down by
    `ryoku/shell/deploy.sh`. `ryoku track unstable` sets this up for testers;
    the deploy records the checkout and the commit it laid down under
    `~/.local/state/ryoku/`, which is how `ryoku` finds it again.

`ryoku update` detects which world it is in, so the same command is correct on
both.

chunks.title: The ryoku command > When doctor cannot fix it: `--report`
chunks.text:
```bash
ryoku doctor --report        # writes ~/.local/state/ryoku/doctor-report.txt
ryoku doctor --report bug.txt
```

The report bundles the findings with system state (disk and snapshot health,
failed units, recent journal errors, package and channel state, session
environment, GPU and display drivers) into one text file to attach to a bug
report. It contains no passwords or keys.

chunks.title: The ryoku command > When you want it to reason: `--explain`
chunks.text:
`ryoku doctor --explain` sends that same report to a cloud model and prints its
root-cause analysis and fix steps.

`--explain` is strictly advisory and read-only: it never runs anything, so
  a wrong answer can only mislead. It is opt-in and uses your own key;
  nothing is sent unless you set one.

Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works. Defaults target Groq:

```bash

ryoku doctor --explain
```

chunks.title: The ryoku command > Window manager
chunks.text:
- `ryoku wm status` names the running window manager and its provider;
  `ryoku wm caps` lists what it can do.
- `ryoku wm use ` switches window manager: it installs that desktop
  variant if needed, previews anything the target cannot honour, and tells you
  to log out and pick it at the greeter. The one you leave stays installed
  unless you add `--remove-previous`. The Compositor tab on the window
  manager page of Ryoku Settings does the same.

chunks.text:
The small tools behind keybinds and Settings pages. All on `$PATH`, all fine
to call directly:

Command | What it does

`ryoku-clamshell` | The lid-switch daemon: closes to an external display on AC, suspends otherwise.

chunks.title: Terminal commands > Overview
chunks.text:
Everything Ryoku does from a keybind or a Settings page is also a command, so
anything the desktop can do, a terminal (or a script of yours) can do too. This
page is the map. The commands that matter most on a daily driver come first;
the rest is reference.

chunks.title: Terminal commands > `ryoku-shell`, the desktop's remote control
chunks.text:
Every surface the shell draws answers to `ryoku-shell `, which is what
the keybinds call. Useful from a terminal when scripting or diagnosing:

chunks.title: Terminal commands > `ryoku-shell`, the desktop's remote control
chunks.text: Command | What it does `ryoku-shell launcher` | Toggle the app launcher. `ryoku-shell ask` | Open the Ask bar (`ask chat` and `ask tools` open a mode). `ryoku-shell quicksettings` | Toggle quick settings. `ryoku-shell clipboard` | Open the clipboard history. `ryoku-shell overview` | Toggle the workspace overview. `ryoku-shell lock` | Lock the session (`lock status` reports `locked` or `unlocked`). `ryoku-shell visualizer` | Toggle the desktop audio visualizer (`visualizer-overlay` raises it above windows). `ryoku-shell voice` | Toggle voice typing. `ryoku-shell hub open` | Open Ryoku Settings. `ryoku-shell theme ` | Apply a color scheme. `ryoku-shell audio up / down / mute` | Nudge the default output. `ryoku-shell brightness <±n>` | Nudge screen brightness. `ryoku-shell bar ...`, `ryoku-shell dock ...` | Arrange the bar and the dock without touching JSON; see below. `ryoku-shell ping` /

chunks.title: Terminal commands > `ryoku-shell`, the desktop's remote control
chunks.text:
`status` | Is the daemon alive, and what does it know. `ryoku-shell reload` | Reload the shell.

The bar and dock verbs are validated against the same widget catalogue the
settings panels use:

```bash
ryoku-shell bar list
ryoku-shell bar move clock --section right --after media
ryoku-shell bar hide battery
ryoku-shell bar position bottom
ryoku-shell dock pin org.kitty
ryoku-shell dock autohide on
```

chunks.title: Terminal commands > The five that matter
chunks.text:
Command | What it does
`ryoku update` | Bring Ryoku current, re-lay its config, self-heal, reload. The one maintenance command.
`ryoku doctor` | Find and fix stateful drift. Safe to run any time; `--check` changes nothing.
`ryoku status` | Channel, version, waiting packages, snapshot count. `--json` for scripts.
`ryoku rollback` | List releases and snapshots; `--to ` moves back to a release.
`ryoku recovery` | Last resort: restore the stable channel and redeploy, whatever state the box is in.

If something feels wrong, the order is `ryoku doctor`, then `ryoku update`,
then `ryoku rollback`. `recovery` is for a machine that cannot help itself.
Every `ryoku` command is covered in depth on The ryoku command.

chunks.title: Terminal commands > Wallpapers: `ryogami`
chunks.text:
Command | What it does
`ryogami wallpaper ui` | Open the wallpaper picker.
`ryogami wallpaper random` | A random wallpaper with a random transition.
`ryogami wallpaper set ` | Set a wallpaper, image or video. `--screen ` targets one display, `--workspace` the current workspace.
`ryogami upscale start ` | Upscale an image (`status` and `cancel` follow it).

chunks.title: Terminal commands > Where these live
chunks.text:
The `ryoku` CLI is Go under `ryoku/cli/`; the shell daemon and its verbs are
`ryoku/shell/ipc/`; Ryogami is `ryoku/shell/ryogami/`; the `ryoku-cmd-*`
helpers are scripts in `ryoku/shell/scripts/`; hardware tools live in
`system/hardware/`. Every one of them ships in the packages, so a script that
works on your machine works on any Ryoku install.

chunks.title: Convert a machine you already have > Choose what you install
chunks.text: The plan screen shows the same choices as the ISO installer:

chunks.title: Convert a machine you already have > Choose what you install
chunks.text: - Window manager: Hyprland or niri (Void is niri only; Wayfire is experimental on Arch and CachyOS). - Web browser: Firefox (recommended), Chromium, Zen on Arch and CachyOS, or none. - Login shell: Fish (recommended), Zsh or Bash. A supported shell you already use is kept. - File manager: Files (Nautilus, recommended because Ryoku's stash menu lives in its right-click menu), Dolphin or Thunar. One you already have is kept. - Rashin: Ryoku's AI agent. It runs the Hermes agent, and the first login opens the Hermes setup unless Hermes is already installed. On Fedora and Void it is part of the desktop package. - Apps: the Ryoku apps first (Ryotunes, Ryoport, RyoManager), then the terminal tools, media, gaming and service rows. Kitty, Neovim and btop are required because desktop features open them. - CachyOS kernel and tuning: only on plain Arch. Off by default. After a mirror check it adds

chunks.title: Convert a machine you already have > Choose what you install
chunks.text:
the CachyOS repositories and kernel (the Arch kernel stays as a fallback), system tuning, sched-ext schedulers, ananicy-cpp and CachyOS Proton. When the mirror is unreachable or the CPU lacks x86-64-v3 it says so and points at Ryostore instead of failing.

The developer toolchain (Go, Node.js, Python tools and mise) stays behind its
own Developer toolchain toggle here, off by default. Packages you leave out
are recorded in `~/.local/state/ryoku/provisioned` unless you already had them,
so `ryoku update` and `ryoku doctor` never add them later.

chunks.title: Convert a machine you already have > Flags and variables
chunks.text:
Pass options after `bash -s --`:

Flag | Variable | What it does
`--dry-run` |  | Print every command it would run and change nothing.
`--yes` |  | Run the plan with no prompts.
`--uninstall` |  | Reverse a previous conversion (see [Reversible](#reversible)).
`--compositor ` |  | Pick the window manager variant the host edition ships.
`--browser ` | `RYOKU_BROWSER` | `firefox`, `chromium`, `zen` or `none`.
`--shell ` | `RYOKU_LOGIN_SHELL` | `fish`, `zsh` or `bash`.
`--file-manager ` | `RYOKU_FILE_MANAGER` | `nautilus`, `dolphin` or `thunar`.
`--rashin=false` | `RYOKU_RASHIN=0` | Leave out Rashin.
`--without ` | `RYOKU_WITHOUT` | Leave out apps by id, for example `ryotunes,ryoport`.
`--cachyos-layer` | `RYOKU_CACHYOS_LAYER=1` | Add the CachyOS layer (plain Arch only).

For example, an unattended niri install with Dolphin and without Rashin,
Ryotunes and Ryoport:

chunks.title: Convert a machine you already have > Flags and variables
chunks.text:
```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ryoku-dev/ryoku/main/ryoku-shell-installer/install.sh \
  | bash -s -- --yes --compositor niri --file-manager dolphin --rashin=false --without ryotunes,ryoport
```

A full dry run that touches nothing:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ryoku-dev/ryoku/main/ryoku-shell-installer/install.sh \
  | bash -s -- --dry-run
```

To fetch the installer and its payload from a specific git ref instead of
`main`, set `RYOKU_SHELL_REF`. The ref also picks the package channel on Fedora
(`main` uses stable, `unstable-dev` uses testing):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ryoku-dev/ryoku/main/ryoku-shell-installer/install.sh \
  | RYOKU_SHELL_REF= bash
```

Choices that are not available on the host edition are refused before `sudo`.
Zen and the AUR rows (LocalSend, Voxtype) are not available on Void or Fedora.

chunks.title: Convert a machine you already have > Overview
chunks.text:
Already running Linux? You do not need the ISO. One command converts an
existing Arch, CachyOS, Void (glibc) or Fedora® 44/45 system into Ryoku in
place, and the same tool undoes it. Everything it touches is backed up first,
your desktops and files stay put, and Ryoku is layered on top rather than
installed over you. It never partitions a disk.

Starting from a clean disk or a new machine instead? Boot the signed ISO; see
Install Ryoku.

The script installer rewrites your desktop configuration and is still being
tested across hardware and setups. Back up first, run the dry run, and prefer a
machine you can afford to reinstall.

chunks.title: Convert a machine you already have > Reversible
chunks.text:
The conversion can be undone. Run the one-liner again with `--uninstall`:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ryoku-dev/ryoku/main/ryoku-shell-installer/install.sh \
  | bash -s -- --uninstall
```

If the `ryoku-shell-install` binary is still on your `PATH`,
`ryoku-shell-install --uninstall` does the same thing. The bootstrap above
always works because it fetches the installer again.

Uninstall walks the conversion backwards:

chunks.title: Convert a machine you already have > Reversible
chunks.text:
1. Removes the Ryoku packages in one transaction (`ryoku-desktop` depends on
   the rest, so the package manager orders the removal).
2. Drops the Ryoku repository, keeping the original configuration beside it.
3. Walks the backup chain newest to oldest, running each `restore.sh` with
   a confirmation prompt, which puts every saved config back and re-enables
   the services and display manager it disabled. Decline one and the walk
   stops there, because the chain only makes sense in order.

Session packages (SDDM, PipeWire, NetworkManager and so on) stay installed:
they may predate Ryoku, and removing them can lock you out of a login. Your
backup directories are kept too; delete them once you are sure.

To roll back only the most recent conversion, run that run's own restore
script: `bash ~/.local/state/ryoku/shell-install/backup-/restore.sh`.

chunks.title: Convert a machine you already have > The one-liner
chunks.text:
Run this as your normal user, not root. The script calls `sudo` only when it
needs elevation.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ryoku-dev/ryoku/main/ryoku-shell-installer/install.sh | bash
```

`install.sh` is a small bootstrap: it detects the package manager (pacman,
XBPS, dnf, or apt for the Debian source build), checks for `x86_64`, downloads
the `ryoku-shell-install` binary, verifies its SHA256 against a committed
checksum, and hands it your terminal. Every real decision lives in that
interactive installer. See Verifying downloads for the
verification path.

chunks.title: Convert a machine you already have > What is touched and what is left alone
chunks.text:
Left alone | Changed only with your toggle
Desktop environments (GNOME, KDE, Cinnamon, Xfce) stay installed and selectable at the login screen | Rival Quickshell shells are uninstalled
niri and sway stay installed as fallback sessions | Conflicting daemons are disabled, never uninstalled
Your files and personal data | The old display manager is disabled, not removed, in favour of SDDM
Software you already had, even if you leave it out of the plan | The Ryoku repository and keyring are added, and dropped again on uninstall

Every config the installer touches is copied, never deleted. Originals of
system files are kept as `*.pre-ryoku`, and per-run copies live in the backup
directory with their `restore.sh`. Your monitor layout and keyboard are carried
over from your existing setup so your screens and keys come back the way you
had them.

chunks.title: Convert a machine you already have > What it does
chunks.text:
The installer is a TUI in the ISO installer's visual language. It scans,
shows the plan, and writes nothing until you confirm.

Detects your GPU and Secure Boot state, the display manager and network
    stack, installed desktops, rival Quickshell shells, known rices,
    conflicting user daemons, any plain Hyprland, niri or sway setup to migrate
    from, an Omarchy install to retire, your keyboard and monitor layout, and
    an interrupted previous run to resume.

The choices above, then the migration toggles: NVIDIA drivers, switch the
    login screen to SDDM with the Ryoku greeter, NetworkManager, remove rival
    shells, disable conflicting daemons, retire an Omarchy repo, carry over
    your monitor layout, AUR extras and the developer toolchain.

chunks.title: Convert a machine you already have > What it does
chunks.text:
Before the first change, every config the plan touches is copied to
    `~/.local/state/ryoku/shell-install/backup-/` with a generated
    `restore.sh`. The script grows a line per saved item, so a kill at any
    moment still leaves a script that undoes what happened so far.

Trusts the signed Ryoku repository for the host (pacman, XBPS or RPM),
    installs the desktop, your window manager variant, your file manager, the
    Ryoku apps and Rashin you kept, and on plain Arch the CachyOS layer when
    you asked for it. Then it wires up SDDM, the greeter and NetworkManager.

Lays down `~/.config`, sets the browser and files roles, hides a
    deselected Ryoport, leaves the first-login notes, runs `ryoku doctor` and
    verifies. Interrupted? Run it again: completed steps are recorded in
    `~/.local/state/ryoku/shell-install-state.json`, so it resumes where it
    stopped.

chunks.title: Convert a machine you already have > What it does
chunks.text:
When it finishes, reboot into the Ryoku login screen. From there it is an
ordinary Ryoku machine: `ryoku update` keeps it current and `ryoku doctor`
heals it. Continue with First boot.

chunks.title: Customization Inventory > Files that are yours
chunks.text:
Ryoku never overwrites these on an update:

File | What it is for
`~/.config/ryoku/user_edits/` | Every change you make in Ryoku Settings, laid back over the shipped config on each update. `ryoku reset` hands a file back.
`~/.config/hypr/user.lua`, `~/.config/niri/user.kdl` | Your own window-manager overrides, loaded last.
`monitors_user.lua`, `monitors_user.kdl` | Hand-pinned displays.
`~/.config/kitty/user.conf`, `~/.config/fish/user.fish` | Per-app overrides.
`~/.config/ryoku/plugins.json` | Plugin placement and settings.

`ryoku owner ` tells you which class any config file belongs to and where
your change should go; see The ryoku command.

chunks.title: Customization Inventory > Overview
chunks.text:
This is a map of the repo paths that ship Ryoku's behavior and where they land

`docs/structure.md`;
this page is the overview.

The packages copy the base config to `/usr/share/ryoku/config`, and
`ryoku materialize` lays it into `~/.config`, replacing Ryoku-owned files but
never touching your own overrides. See Customize for the
override files and Updates for how updates apply.

chunks.title: Customize > Make it yours
chunks.text:
The knobs most people reach for first live in Ryoku Settings (`Mod+,`), and
the first-run welcome offers the same handful inline:

- Interface scale. If everything looks oversized on first boot, ease the
  interface scale down and the whole shell resizes. This is the single most
  common first-boot fix.
- The bar. QS Bar is the default; Orpheus, Sumi, Kairos, Shima, Python and
  Nomarchy are the other styles. Bar Studio arranges the rails, zones and
  widgets.
- Desktop widgets. Right-click the wallpaper and choose Edit desktop to
  add, move and resize widgets, set up depth and parallax, or add a
  visualizer.
- Colors. The palette follows your wallpaper by default (derived by
  `matugen`), so a new wallpaper recolors the whole desktop; lock a fixed
  palette instead if you prefer. See Theming.

chunks.title: Customize > Make it yours
chunks.text:
Deeper window work (rounding, blur, gaps, animations) stays in Ryoku Settings
too. This page picks up where the GUI stops.

chunks.title: Customize > Manual monitor pinning
chunks.text:
For everyday display changes, use Settings > Displays (see [Displays &
hardware](/docs/hardware)). It writes the generated `monitors.lua` (Hyprland)
or `monitors.kdl` (niri), which `ryoku-monitor` also rewrites once per machine
and on hotplug or GPU reset.

When you need a layout the page cannot express, a fake-EDID display that needs
a forced mode, a forced modeline, or a specific position, write
`~/.config/hypr/monitors_user.lua` or `~/.config/niri/monitors_user.kdl`
instead. It loads after the generated file, so your pins win, and updates never
touch it. On Hyprland a template ships at
`~/.config/hypr/monitors_user.lua.example`.

chunks.title: Customize > Overview
chunks.text:
Most customization happens in Ryoku Settings (the Hub), opened with `Mod+,`.
This page is the other half: the plain files Ryoku reserves for you in
`~/.config/`, which `ryoku update` never touches. Reach for them when the GUI
does not cover what you want, or when you would rather edit text than click.

Displays, input, keybinds, the bar, the desktop and more, applied live.

Color schemes, the matugen palette, wallpapers and rices.

Displays have both paths: tune them in Settings > Displays (see [Displays &
  hardware](/docs/hardware)), and hand-pin the stubborn ones in
  `monitors_user.lua` or `monitors_user.kdl`, below.

chunks.title: Customize > Per-app settings
chunks.text:
Each app under `ryoku/apps//` keeps its native format under its own
directory; there is no Lua wrapper for a tool that reads its own config. Where an
app ships a base file, drop your changes in the paired override file so an update
cannot clobber them:

App | Shipped file | Override file
Kitty | `~/.config/kitty/kitty.conf` | `~/.config/kitty/user.conf`
Fish | `~/.config/fish/config.fish` | `~/.config/fish/user.fish`
Starship | `~/.config/starship.toml` | edit in place
Neovim | `~/.config/nvim/` | LazyVim's own override paths
Yazi | `~/.config/yazi/yazi.toml` | edit in place
Fastfetch | `~/.config/fastfetch/` | edit in place

chunks.title: Customize > Personal compositor overrides
chunks.text:
Each window manager reads one file of yours last, so it wins over both the
shipped defaults and anything Ryoku Settings writes. It is seeded once and never
touched by `ryoku materialize` or an update.

`~/.config/hypr/user.lua` loads last. The order, from
    `ryoku/hyprland/hyprland.lua`, is:

1. `modules.env`, then `keyboard.lua`.
    2. The generated drop-ins `gpu.lua` and `monitors.lua`, then your
       `monitors_user.lua` if present.
    3. The base modules (`displays`, `input`, `touchpad`, `decoration`,
       `animations`, `binds`, `window_rules`, `autostart` and the rest).
    4. `settings.lua`, written by the Hub.
    5. The power saver, when Performance follows the power profile.
    6. `user.lua`: yours, loaded last, wins.

```lua
    -- ~/.config/hypr/user.lua
    hl.bind("SUPER", "U", "exec, kitty -e htop")
    hl.windowrule("float", "class:^(pavucontrol)$")
    ```

chunks.title: Customize > Personal compositor overrides
chunks.text:
Use the `hl` API the modules use (`hl.bind`, `hl.windowrule`, the keyword
    setters) rather than shelling out to `hyprctl`.

`~/.config/niri/user.kdl` is the last include in `config.kdl`. Before it
    come the machine seeds (`keyboard.kdl`, the generated `gpu.kdl` and
    `monitors.kdl`, your `monitors_user.kdl`), then the Hub's generated
    `settings.kdl` and `rebinds.kdl`. The last include wins for a value set
    twice, and a chord you bind here replaces the shipped one.

```kdl
    // ~/.config/niri/user.kdl
    binds {
        Mod+Shift+T { spawn "kitty"; }
    }
    ```

Never hand-edit `settings.kdl` or `rebinds.kdl`; they are rewritten from
    the Hub.

chunks.title: Customize > Reloading after a change
chunks.text:
After editing a file by hand:

```bash
ryoku reload
```

This restarts the shell and reloads the window manager. Ryoku Settings applies
its own changes live and does not need a reload.

chunks.title: Customize > See also
chunks.text:
The GUI for everything above, and the panels this page complements.

Color schemes, palette, wallpapers and rices.

The GUI display, GPU, input, and power controls.

The shipped binds your override file can replace.

chunks.title: Customize > What survives an update
chunks.text:
`ryoku materialize` clobbers the
files Ryoku ships and prunes files a past release shipped but this one dropped.
It never touches files Ryoku only seeds once or never shipped, which is
what makes `user.lua`, `user.kdl`, the `monitors_user` files,
`kitty/user.conf`, `fish/user.fish` and your own additions survive every
update. Changes you make in Ryoku Settings are kept in
`~/.config/ryoku/user_edits` and laid back over the shipped config on every
update.

The generated drop-ins (`monitors` and `gpu`) are seeded only when absent and
are never clobbered or pruned, so an update never resets your display layout or
GPU pin.

Editing a shipped file in place (anything in the "shipped file" column above,
  or `hypr/hypridle.conf`, and the other base configs) is reset on the next
  `ryoku materialize`. Put lasting changes in an override file, or in your
  `user.lua` or `user.kdl`.

chunks.title: Dual-boot with Windows > After install
chunks.text:
The Limine boot menu appears at power-on with entries for Ryoku and
Windows; pick whichever you want. If Windows does not appear, boot Ryoku and
run `ryoku doctor`, then see Troubleshoot.

chunks.title: Dual-boot with Windows > "I press Tab and nothing happens"
chunks.text:
On the Disk layout step, Tab only continues once the layout is
installable. When it is blocked, the screen shows a red `⚠` line with the
reason. The usual causes:

Select a partition in the list and use `←`/`→` to give Ryoku room, or make
    room in Windows first (Step 2).

The reasons are listed under each partition. The usual one is a Windows
    volume that is hibernated or marked dirty: turn off Fast Startup, run a
    full shutdown, and try again. BitLocker-locked volumes are not shrunk.

Alongside installs need UEFI and GPT. Boot the USB in UEFI mode, or press
    `esc` and choose Erase whole disk on a dedicated drive.

Ryoku needs at least 32 GiB. Pick a larger disk.

chunks.title: Dual-boot with Windows > Overview
chunks.text:
Ryoku installs alongside Windows on a single disk. Pick Install alongside
at the installer's Disk strategy step and Ryoku goes into free
(unallocated) space. If the disk has none, the installer can shrink one
partition for you to make room. Your other partitions are kept as they are,
and the Limine boot menu lists Ryoku and Windows.

Shrinking a partition changes your Windows disk. Back up anything you cannot
lose before you start, whichever way you make the room.

chunks.title: Dual-boot with Windows > See also
chunks.text:
The full install walkthrough, from ISO to first boot.

Boot, login and disk recovery when something goes wrong.

chunks.title: Dual-boot with Windows > Step 1: Disable Secure Boot
chunks.text:
Reboot into your firmware setup (usually `F2`, `Del` or `F12` at power-on),
turn Secure Boot off, save and exit. See Install Ryoku for
writing the USB.

chunks.title: Dual-boot with Windows > Step 2: Make room, either way
chunks.text:
Skip ahead to Step 3. When the disk has no free space, the Disk layout
    step lists the partitions it can shrink (NTFS, ext4 and btrfs). Select one
    and use `←` and `→` to set how much space Ryoku gets. The installer shrinks
    the filesystem first and the partition second, touches only that one
    partition, and stops at the first sign of trouble.

In Windows press `Win + X`, open Disk Management, right-click your
    Windows (C:) volume and choose Shrink Volume. Shrink it by at least the
    space Ryoku needs (64 GiB is a comfortable amount). The Unallocated
    space that appears after the Windows partition is where Ryoku goes. Then
    shut Windows down fully.

chunks.title: Dual-boot with Windows > Step 3: Install alongside Windows
chunks.text:
Boot the Ryoku USB in UEFI mode. In the installer:

At Target disk, choose the disk that holds Windows.

At Disk strategy, pick Install alongside Windows (or Install
    alongside (keep existing OS) on a disk with another system). Nothing is
    written until the final Review step.

The Disk layout step shows the free space Ryoku will use, or the
    partition it will shrink and by how much. Adjust swap if you like, then
    press Tab to continue to Review. Review states exactly what will be
    created and kept; confirm there to install.

Ryoku creates its 2 GiB boot partition and root in the free region, installs
Limine with an entry for Windows, and leaves the Windows partitions as they
are (apart from the one you chose to shrink).

chunks.title: Dual-boot with Windows > Step 3: Install alongside Windows
chunks.text:
A second, empty GPT drive with free space and no EFI partition of its own works
too: the installer offers Install in the free space, creates a new EFI
partition and root there, and leaves every existing partition untouched.

chunks.title: Dual-boot with Windows > What you need
chunks.text:
- UEFI and GPT. Boot the Ryoku USB in UEFI mode, not BIOS/CSM/legacy. A
  UEFI Windows install already uses GPT.
- Room for Ryoku: at least a 20 GiB root plus a 2 GiB boot partition and
  your swap size. 64 GiB or more is comfortable. The whole disk must be at
  least 32 GiB.
- Windows shut down cleanly. Turn off Fast Startup in Windows (Control
  Panel > Power Options > Choose what the power buttons do, then untick
  Turn on fast startup) and use Shut down, not Restart or Sleep. A
  hibernated NTFS volume cannot be shrunk safely, and the installer refuses to
  touch it.
- BitLocker: suspend it in Windows first and keep your recovery key. With
  BitLocker on, booting Windows from the Ryoku menu asks for the recovery key.

No second disk is required. If you would rather keep the two systems fully
separate, put Ryoku on its own drive and choose Erase whole disk there.

chunks.title: Extras > From a terminal
chunks.text:
`ryostore-install` drives everything from a shell. Bundle and item ids are the
ones in the catalogue (for example `gaming`, `developer-essentials`,
`cachyos-layer`).

```bash

chunks.title: Extras > Install a bundle
chunks.text:
Open Ryostore from the launcher, or press Browse RyoStore on the
    Add-ons page of Ryoku Settings. Bundles sit beside lockscreens, rices, bar
    styles and plugins; each one shows what it contains and its live install
    state.

Open a bundle to see its items, then Install. Ryostore opens a floating
    terminal so `sudo` has a real prompt, and streams progress as each item
    lands.

Items report present or absent live, so the bundle updates as it installs.
    Remove it the same way. Installed bundles are also listed on the Add-ons
    page, where you can repair or remove them.

The catalogue lives in the
`ryostore` repository. Ryostore fetches
and caches it, and the actuator, `ryostore-install`, only ever reads that cache.

chunks.title: Extras > Install an entire bundle.
chunks.text: ryostore-install install bundle gaming

chunks.title: Extras > Install or remove a single item.
chunks.text:
ryostore-install install item gaming steam
ryostore-install remove item gaming steam

chunks.title: Extras > Overview
chunks.text:
Ryoku keeps its core deliberately small: a terminal, an editor, a browser, a
file manager, and the shell that ties them together. Everything else, a game
launcher, a streaming rig, a full dev stack, is added on demand as a
bundle: a curated set of software installed together, so adding a whole
workflow is one click instead of an afternoon of hunting packages and their
drivers.

Bundles install *software*. For the small desktop widgets you place on the
wallpaper, see Plugins, a separate system that lives in the
same store.

chunks.title: Extras > Remove a bundle's package items.
chunks.text:
ryostore-install remove bundle gaming
```

Set `RYOSTORE_DRYRUN=1` to print the plan without touching the system:

```bash
RYOSTORE_DRYRUN=1 ryostore-install install bundle gaming
```

The actuator publishes a JSON report per bundle under
`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/ryostore/`, which is how Ryostore and the Add-ons page update
in place while a bundle installs or removes.

chunks.text:

chunks.title: Extras > What a bundle contains
chunks.text:
A bundle is a list of items. You never write or see the routing; the actuator
picks the right path per item.

Kind | What it is | How it installs
**package** | A distribution package. | Installed with your edition's package manager. On Arch, a package that is not in the official repositories is built from the AUR. Packages are batched.
**script** | A small installer from the catalogue's `installers/`, for tools no repository carries. | Run with `bash`, then detected by a `command -v` check.
**plugin** | A shell [plugin](/docs/plugins), such as a desktop widget. | Fetched into `~/.local/share/ryoku/plugins//`; turn it on and place it from the Add-ons page.
**Nautilus pack** | Right-click actions for Nautilus. | Installed by Ryostore and tracked under `~/.local/share/ryoku/nautilus/`.

chunks.title: Extras > What a bundle contains
chunks.text:
Bundles can declare what they need first: the `multilib` repository (Steam's
32-bit libraries), the CachyOS repository, or the 32-bit GPU drivers for your
hardware. The actuator sets those up before it routes any package.

script items are arbitrary installers, so removing a bundle does not
  reverse them; uninstall those tools by hand. Removing package items never
  drops anything another installed package still needs. Removing a plugin
  deletes its files but keeps your placement in `~/.config/ryoku/plugins.json`,
  so reinstalling drops it back where you had it.

chunks.title: FAQ > Overview
chunks.text:
Quick answers to the things people ask first. Each one links to the page that
covers it in full: start here, then follow the link when you want the detail.

Yes, Ryoku is an Omarchy alternative from the same lineage: an opinionated,
    keyboard-driven desktop that works on day one. What differs is what Ryoku
    ships on top: its own Quickshell UI on Hyprland or niri, Ryoku Settings,
    Ryostore and a plugin host, four editions (Arch, CachyOS, Void, Fedora),
    and a single-source system driven by the `ryoku` CLI (`update`,
    `rollback`, `doctor`). See Omarchy heritage.

chunks.title: FAQ > Overview
chunks.text:
Run `ryoku update`, or press Update now in Ryoku Settings > Updates.
    It takes a snapshot, brings the system current from the signed Ryoku
    repository, re-lays the base config with `ryoku materialize`, and reloads
    the shell. Stable boxes follow releases; `ryoku track unstable` follows the
    testing channel and `ryoku track stable` goes back. See CLI for
    the command reference and Updates for the full model.

On a btrfs root every `ryoku update` is wrapped in a snapper pre/post
    snapshot pair. Run `ryoku rollback` to list snapshots and pick one, or
    `ryoku rollback ` to go straight to it. The same snapshots are selectable
    from the Limine boot menu, so even a system that will not boot back into
    Hyprland can be recovered from the bootloader. The full rollback and recovery
    path is in Updates.

chunks.title: FAQ > Overview
chunks.text:
Ryoku's base config is laid down under `~/.config` by `ryoku materialize`,
    which runs on every update. Your own changes go in the dedicated override
    files that updates never touch: `~/.config/hypr/user.lua`,
    `~/.config/kitty/user.conf`, `~/.config/fish/user.fish`, and
    `~/.config/hypr/monitors_user.lua`. Editing shipped files in place works too,
    but the override files are the update-safe way to customize. See
    Customize.

Pick a color scheme in the wallpaper picker's settings (`Mod + W`, then
    `Shift + S`, Theme), or apply a rice (Default and NOC ship with Ryoku)
    from the picker's Rices tab. `Ctrl + D` inside the picker downloads
    wallpapers, and `Mod + Shift + W` sets a random one. By default the palette
    follows the wallpaper. See Theming.

chunks.title: FAQ > Overview
chunks.text:
Open Ryostore from the launcher (or Browse RyoStore on the Add-ons page
    of Ryoku Settings) and install a bundle; the Gaming bundle brings Wine and
    Proton, launchers and overlays. You can still use the distribution's
    package manager and Flatpak directly, or the launcher's `>install`
    provider. See Extras.

Right-click the desktop and pick Edit desktop, add a widget, then drag
    it where you want it. Right-click a widget for its own settings. More
    widgets install from Ryostore. See Plugins.

Yes. The installers ask for the browser, login shell, file manager and
    Rashin, and list every optional app (Ryotunes, Ryoport, RyoManager, the
    terminal tools and more) so you can untick what you do not want. Whatever
    you leave out stays out after updates. See Install Ryoku.

chunks.title: FAQ > Overview
chunks.text:
Yes. Ryoku is the desktop, not the kernel. On Arch, the installer's CachyOS
    layer and the Ryostore CachyOS Layer bundle add the CachyOS kernel and
    tuning while the stock Arch kernel stays as a fallback. See
    Kernels.

Open Ryoku Settings > Input. It sets keyboard layout, key repeat, and
    pointer/touchpad behavior, and applies the change live. The chosen layout is
    also carried into a fresh session. See Hardware and
    Settings.

Set resolution, scale, and rotation in Ryoku Settings > Displays. Laptop
    (eDP) panels expose only their native resolution, so use the scale options to
    get a smaller desktop. For graphics, Displays > GPU pins the render
    device; it is read at login, so log out and back in to apply it. See
    Hardware and Troubleshoot.

chunks.title: FAQ > Overview
chunks.text:
Run `ryoku reload` to restart the shell, then check
    `~/.local/state/ryoku-shell.log`. The usual causes are an update that left
    the shell out of sync (run `ryoku update` again, or `ryoku rollback`), a Lua
    error in a hand-edited `user.lua` or `monitors_user.lua`, or a corrupt
    generated `monitors.lua`/`gpu.lua` that `ryoku doctor` repairs. The full
    checklist is in Troubleshoot.

Yes, on Arch, CachyOS, Void and Fedora. The script installer scans your
    machine, shows the same choices as the ISO plus its migration toggles,
    backs up every config it touches (with a `restore.sh`), adds the signed
    repository, installs the Ryoku packages and materializes the config. It is
    reversible with `--uninstall`. See Convert.

chunks.title: FAQ > Overview
chunks.text:
Yes, on a single disk or a dedicated one. Ryoku reuses your existing EFI
    partition and installs into unallocated free space. It never resizes
    Windows, so you shrink the Windows partition first (Windows Disk
    Management) to make room, then pick Install alongside Windows in the
    installer. If the Disk layout step will not let you press Tab, there is
    no free space or no EFI partition yet. Full steps:
    Dual-boot with Windows.

No. The Rashin daemon binds `127.0.0.1` only and its knowledge vault is
    plain markdown on your disk. Questions go to the model provider you choose
    in Hermes, nothing else. You can leave Rashin out in the installer or turn
    it off later. See Rashin and Security.

chunks.title: FAQ > Overview
chunks.text:
Import the release key, confirm its fingerprint, then `gpg --verify` the ISO
    against its `.sig` and `sha256sum -c` its `.sha256`. Every ISO and every
    `[ryoku]` package is signed by `Ryoku Releases `. The
    exact commands and the fingerprint to check against are in
    Security.

chunks.text:
Logs, `ryoku doctor`, recovery, and how to file a useful bug.

The full `ryoku` command reference behind every answer above.

chunks.title: First boot > If nothing draws
chunks.text:
If the bar, the launcher or Ryoku Settings do not appear, switch to a TTY
(`Ctrl + Alt + F2`), log in, then restart the shell and read its log:

```bash
ryoku reload
tail -n 80 ~/.local/state/ryoku-shell.log
ryoku doctor
```

Troubleshoot covers the common boot and login issues.

chunks.title: First boot > Keys worth pressing first
chunks.text:
`Mod + Return` opens the terminal role, kitty unless you changed it.

`Mod + Space` opens the launcher. Type to filter, Enter to launch.

`Mod + ,` opens Ryoku Settings, the control center for the whole desktop.

`Mod + K` opens Kit: every keybind, every Ryoku command, your phone and
    dev tools behind one search field.

chunks.title: First boot > Next steps
chunks.text:
- Navigation: open, focus, move and tile windows across
  workspaces.
- Desktop tour: the shell surfaces and where things live.
- Keybindings: the shipped reference, grouped by purpose.
- Customize: wallpapers, themes and your own overrides.

chunks.title: First boot > Overview
chunks.text:
After install, the machine reboots to the Ryoku login screen. Log in with the
user you created; the session starts the window manager you picked in the
installer.

chunks.title: First boot > What happens at the first login
chunks.text: - The Default rice is applied. Ryoku ships two rices, Default and NOC. Default sets the first look, including its own wallpaper, and the desktop recolours from that wallpaper. NOC is one click away in the rice workshop (see Themes). - The welcome tour opens once. It walks through the handful of keys that open almost everything and lets you pick the interface scale, the bar and the desktop widgets, previewed live. It shows on a fresh install, after the script installer, and once more when an update reworks it. - The Hermes setup opens when you kept Rashin. If you answered yes to Rashin in the installer, a terminal opens once the machine is online and runs the Hermes setup: it installs the Hermes agent, connects it and asks you to pick a provider. Offline? It waits for a later login. You can run it again any time from Set up Hermes agent on the Rashin page of Ryoku Settings, or with

chunks.title: First boot > What happens at the first login
chunks.text: `ryoku-rashin setup` in a terminal.

chunks.title: First boot > What you see
chunks.text:
- The frame. A rounded screen border, the desktop's signature chrome.
  Panels grow out of it instead of floating on top.
- The bar. A fresh install shows QS Bar: the launcher, workspaces, the
  clock, the tray and status. Orpheus, Sumi, Kairos, Shima, Python and
  Nomarchy are the other styles, in the welcome tour and Ryoku Settings.
- The wallpaper from the Default rice, with the desktop widgets you enable
  painted on it.
- No windows yet. Hyprland and niri are tiling window managers, so nothing
  is open until you open it.

`Mod` is `Super` (the Windows or Cmd key on most keyboards).

chunks.title: Displays & hardware > Displays
chunks.text:
Ryoku Settings > Displays is the display control panel. It lists every
connected output and lets you set, per output:

- Resolution and refresh rate
- Scale (fractional scaling for HiDPI panels)
- Rotation
- Position in the layout
- Mirror vs extend
- Named layout profiles you can switch between
- Night light: a warmer tint on demand, from sunset to sunrise, or between hours
  you choose

Applying a change writes the per-machine drop-in generated by `ryoku-monitor`
(`monitors.lua` on Hyprland, `monitors.kdl` on niri). Ryoku rewrites it on
hotplug or a GPU reset, and `ryoku update` never resets it.

chunks.title: Displays & hardware > Displays
chunks.text:
Laptop (eDP) panels expose only their native resolution. To get a smaller
  logical desktop, use the scale options instead of a lower resolution; they
  are labelled with the logical resolution they produce (for example 2048x1280)
  and are the Wayland-correct way to downscale. If `Apply` toasts a rejection,
  the compositor refused that mode or scale; pick one of the offered
  clean-divisor scales.

chunks.title: Displays & hardware > Graphics & Power
chunks.text:
Ryoku Settings > Graphics & Power lists every detected GPU and pins the
primary render device through `ryoku-gpu`. On a hybrid laptop (a discrete NVIDIA
or Radeon beside the CPU's integrated GPU) the integrated GPU is the
battery-friendly default. Pick the discrete or external GPU there to render the
desktop on it instead. Heavy work such as video decoding goes to the strongest
GPU either way.

The GPU pin is read once when the compositor starts, so a change takes effect
  on the next login. Log out and back in to apply it.

The page offers three host graphics modes:

Mode | What it does
Hybrid | No pin; the integrated GPU renders the desktop (best battery).
Performance | Pins the strongest GPU (the discrete one) as the primary renderer.
Passthrough | Pins the integrated GPU alone, freeing the discrete GPU for a virtual machine.

chunks.title: Displays & hardware > Graphics & Power
chunks.text:
From a terminal, `ryoku-gpu` prints what it detected and what it chose:

```bash
ryoku-gpu           # detection plus the current pin and udev-rule state
ryoku-gpu detect    # just the detected GPUs (strongest first)
```

To force the discrete GPU on a laptop against the battery-first default, run
  `RYOKU_GPU_FORCE=1 ryoku-gpu persist`. For a GPU that will not drive the
  desktop, see [Troubleshoot > The wrong GPU is being
  used](/docs/troubleshoot#the-wrong-gpu-is-being-used).

chunks.title: Displays & hardware > Hand-pinning a layout
chunks.text:
When the page cannot express what a stubborn display needs (a fake-EDID monitor
that wants a forced mode or modeline, a precise position), pin it yourself in
`monitors_user.lua` (Hyprland) or `monitors_user.kdl` (niri). It loads after the
generated file, so your pins win, and it is never touched by updates. See
Customize.

chunks.title: Displays & hardware > Input
chunks.text:
Ryoku Settings > Input covers keyboards and pointing devices:

- Keyboard layout (and variant)
- Key repeat rate and delay
- Mouse and touchpad behaviour (speed, natural scroll, tap-to-click, gestures)

The installer carries over the keyboard layout you chose, and the Input page is
where you change it later. Layout changes apply live; `ryoku keyboard apply`
carries the layout to the greeter, the console and the disk passphrase prompt
(see The ryoku command).

chunks.title: Displays & hardware > Overview
chunks.text:
Ryoku profiles your hardware at install time and seeds the right defaults, then
hands you the controls in Ryoku Settings (the Hub), opened with `Mod+,`.
Displays, graphics and power, and input each have their own page. This page is
the map. For hand-editing the underlying files, see
Customize; for every page in full, see
Settings.

chunks.title: Displays & hardware > Power & idle
chunks.text:
An idle session steps down in stages: the screen dims, the session locks, the
displays switch off, and finally the machine suspends. Each stage has its own
timing on battery and on AC, set on the Graphics & Power page alongside the
power profile and the battery charge limit. The same idle policy runs on every
window manager.

The session also locks before sleep or suspend, and restores brightness and the
displays on resume. Alongside it:

- Battery is read through `upower`; the shell surfaces charge and status.
- Brightness keys drive laptop backlights and external DDC monitors alike
  (`ryoku-cmd-brightness`).
- Night light lives on the Displays page and is remembered at your
  chosen color temperature.

chunks.title: Displays & hardware > Quick mirror / extend toggle
chunks.text:
Press `Mod+P` to cycle the displays through internal only, external only and
both. Handy for plugging into a projector or a TV without opening Settings. See
Keybindings for the full bind list.

chunks.title: Displays & hardware > See also
chunks.text:
Every Ryoku Settings panel, in full.

Hand-pin displays and add personal binds in the override files.

Wrong GPU, only one resolution, a display that will not apply.

`Mod+P` and the rest of the shipped binds.

Public ISO availability is tracked on ryoku.dev. You can
also build the image yourself from the monorepo; see
ISO build recipe for the full procedure and the
hardware notes.

A USB stick of at least 8 GB is fine. Flash the ISO with `dd`, balenaEtcher,
or Ventoy.

```bash
chunks.title: Install Ryoku > 3. Try in a VM first (optional)
chunks.text:
Ryoku targets modern desktops and laptops. If you want to walk through the
installer before committing to bare metal, boot the ISO in QEMU/KVM,
VirtualBox, or VMware with at least 16 GB RAM and a 60 GB virtual disk. For
first-class daily use on real hardware, target 32 GB RAM and 80 GB free disk.

chunks.title: Install Ryoku > 4. Boot the installer
chunks.text:
The ISO is a live image with one job: boot the machine and drop you straight
into the Ryoku installer.

The live system logs in as root on `tty1` and starts a small Wayland kiosk
    (`cage`) running a terminal that runs `ryoku-tui`. The serial console and
    the other VTs stay plain root shells for headless or recovery use.

`ryoku-tui` asks, in order: keyboard layout, system locale, time zone,
    network, hardware, hardware profile, graphics mode, window manager, web
    browser, login shell, file manager, Rashin, the CachyOS layer (Arch ISO
    only), Apps & tools, target disk, disk strategy, disk layout, hostname,
    primary user, password and disk encryption. Nothing is written to disk
    until you confirm on the Review screen, and each step can be revisited from
    the rail on the left.

chunks.title: Install Ryoku > 4. Boot the installer
chunks.text:
On confirm, the TUI exports your choices as `RYOKU_*` environment
    variables and runs `ryoku-install`. The same variables can be set by hand
    on the serial console for a headless install; `RYOKU_DRYRUN=1` runs every
    stage without touching the disk.

chunks.title: Install Ryoku > 5. Choose what you install
chunks.text:
The ISOs and the script installer share one list of choices.
Whatever you leave out is recorded in `~/.local/state/ryoku/provisioned`, so
`ryoku update` and `ryoku doctor` never put it back.

Question | Choices | Default
Window manager | Hyprland, niri, Wayfire (experimental; Arch and CachyOS) | Hyprland (niri on Void)
Web browser | Firefox, Chromium, Zen (Arch and CachyOS), none | Firefox
Login shell | Fish, Zsh with Oh My Zsh, Bash with ble.sh | Fish
File manager | Files (Nautilus), Dolphin, Thunar | Nautilus, because Ryoku's stash menu lives in its right-click menu
Rashin | yes or no | yes
CachyOS layer | yes or no, Arch ISO only | no
Apps & tools | every optional app Ryoku ships | all on

chunks.title: Install Ryoku > 5. Choose what you install
chunks.text: - File manager. The one you pick is installed, becomes the files role (the launcher's Files entry and "open folder" actions) and handles folders. You can change the role later in Ryoku Settings. - Rashin. Ryoku's AI agent: Ask on `Alt + Space`, the Rashin window and the bar's AI usage. It runs the Hermes agent, which installs at your first login once the machine is online. Turn it off later on the Rashin page of Ryoku Settings. On Void the desktop package requires it, so the step only explains it. - CachyOS layer. Adds the CachyOS repositories and kernel, with the Arch kernel kept as a boot fallback, plus system tuning, sched-ext schedulers, ananicy-cpp and CachyOS Proton. It needs a network connection, even on an offline ISO, and the install carries on without it when the CachyOS mirror is unreachable. It is the same set as the Ryostore CachyOS Layer bundle; see Kernels. - Apps & tools.

chunks.title: Install Ryoku > 5. Choose what you install
chunks.text: The Ryoku apps come first: Ryotunes (music), Ryoport (VMs, SSH and serial consoles) and RyoManager (system monitor and task manager). Then the terminal tools (Starship, Fastfetch, Yazi, the modern CLI tools eza, bat, fzf and zoxide, the Git tools), media, gaming, system services and developer toolchains. Kitty, Neovim and btop are marked required because desktop features open them.

chunks.title: Install Ryoku > 6. What the backend does
chunks.text:
`ryoku-install` runs the stages below, each in its own file under
`installation/backend/lib/`. It streams its log to stdout and emits
`@@RYOKU_STEP ` sentinels so the TUI can draw staged progress; on success
it prints `@@RYOKU_DONE` and exits 0.

chunks.title: Install Ryoku > 6. What the backend does
chunks.text: Stage | What it does `preflight` | Validate the `RYOKU_*` answers, require root, require UEFI on Arch and CachyOS (Void also installs on legacy BIOS), sanity-check the target disk. `disk` | Partition the target per `RYOKU_DISK_STRATEGY` (`whole` to wipe, `alongside` to dual-boot), create the ESP and root partitions. `luks` | Format and open the root partition as LUKS2, only when `RYOKU_ENCRYPT=1`. `filesystem` | Make the filesystems and create the Btrfs subvolumes (`@`, `@home`, `@snapshots`, optional `@backups`), then mount them. `pacstrap` | Install the base system, microcode and GPU drivers, minus the packages you left out. `configure` | Locale, time zone, hostname, console keymap, the primary user with the login shell you picked, NetworkManager. `deploy` | Add the signed `[ryoku]` repository, then install `ryoku-desktop`, the variant for your window manager, your file manager and the

chunks.title: Install Ryoku > 6. What the backend does
chunks.text:
Ryoku apps and Rashin you kept. Seed the first-login notes: the Default rice, and the Hermes setup when Rashin was kept. Hide a deselected Ryoport for the new user. `drivers` | Wire up the GPU profile (`amd-nvidia`, `amd`, `intel`, or `vm`) and any per-profile services. `cachyos layer` | Arch ISO only, when chosen: add `[cachyos-v3]` and multilib, then one full upgrade that installs the kernel, tuning, schedulers and Proton. `bootloader` | Install Limine with an entry per installed kernel and the Plymouth splash. `aur` | Build and install the AUR set. `snapshots` | Configure snapper, `snap-pac` and `limine-snapper-sync` so updates take pre and post snapshots and Limine lists them in the boot menu.

The GPU and monitor helpers write the compositor's GPU and monitor files on
the first login, so the installer does not run them.

chunks.title: Install Ryoku > 7. Reboot
chunks.text:
When the backend finishes, reboot and remove the USB. The login screen appears;
log in with the user you created.

Continue with First boot for what to expect on the desktop
and the first few keys worth pressing.

chunks.title: Install Ryoku > Hardware notes
chunks.text:
The shipped GPU profiles are `amd-nvidia` (hybrid laptop with NVIDIA + AMD),
`amd`, `intel`, and `vm`. Secure Boot is not configured automatically; the
ISO build recipe tracks the working hardware list
and the harmless chroot warnings you can ignore.

chunks.title: Install Ryoku > Import the release key
chunks.text:
curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ryoku-dev/ryoku/main/keys/ryoku-release-key.pub.asc \
  | gpg --import

chunks.title: Install Ryoku > Overview
chunks.text:
Ryoku ships signed live ISOs for Arch, CachyOS and Void. Boot one, answer a
short series of questions in a terminal installer, and the backend lays the
base system, the Ryoku desktop and the apps you picked, and a Limine boot menu
onto the disk. There is no archinstall in the loop and no hidden JSON: plain
bash runs the stages in order, so you can read the whole thing top to bottom
and follow exactly what happens to the disk.

Installing next to Windows on one disk? See [Dual-boot with
Windows](/docs/dual-boot); you make the free space first. Already running Arch,
CachyOS, Void or Fedora? Convert your machine in place
instead of reinstalling.

chunks.title: Install Ryoku > Show the fingerprint and compare it against the one in the repo
chunks.text: gpg --fingerprint releases@ryoku.dev

chunks.title: Install Ryoku > Verify the ISO against its detached signature
chunks.text:
gpg --verify ryoku--x86_64.iso.sig ryoku--x86_64.iso
```

[Release pipeline](/docs/release-pipeline) has the full walkthrough of what
good output looks like and the offline-keyring path.

See [Verifying downloads](/docs/security) for the signing key, checksums, and
what a good check looks like. The same verification also guards the
[in-place converter](/docs/convert).

chunks.title: Kernels > Add it later
chunks.text:
Open Ryostore, find the CachyOS Layer bundle, and install all of it or pick
single items. It adds the same repositories and packages as the installer.
Reboot to run the new kernel; the stock kernel stays installed and bootable.

Installing a kernel rebuilds every DKMS module against it, so watch for NVIDIA
build errors during the transaction. `/boot` also gains a second kernel image
and initramfs.

chunks.title: Kernels > Get it at install time
chunks.text:
The Arch ISO asks about the CachyOS layer after the Rashin question; the script
installer shows it as a toggle on plain Arch. Both are off by default.

- It needs a network connection, also on an offline ISO. The ISO only offers it
  while the network is up.
- The layer is added after the desktop is installed: the repository helpers
  run first, then one full-upgrade transaction installs the packages, so the
  whole system is current from the network.
- If the CachyOS mirror is unreachable or a step fails, the install carries on
  without the layer and tells you to add it later from Ryostore.
- The boot menu gets a CachyOS kernel entry next to the stock one.

chunks.title: Kernels > Is it still Ryoku?
chunks.text:
Yes. A distribution is defined by its desktop, tooling, repository and
defaults, not by the kernel it boots. With the layer the system stays Ryoku on
the Arch base, with the `[ryoku]` desktop, the `ryoku` CLI and the same
defaults. If you want CachyOS underneath, install the CachyOS edition instead.

chunks.title: Kernels > Overview
chunks.text:
There are three ways to run Ryoku with respect to CachyOS:

Path | What you get | Where
**Ryoku on Arch** | The stock Arch `linux` kernel and the Arch userland | Arch ISO, or the script installer on Arch
**Ryoku on Arch plus the CachyOS layer** | The CachyOS kernel and tuning on top of the Arch userland, with the stock kernel kept as a boot fallback | The **CachyOS layer** question in the Arch ISO or script installer, or the **CachyOS Layer** bundle in Ryostore
**The CachyOS edition** | A full CachyOS system: CachyOS's pacman, its repositories for your CPU tier, `linux-cachyos` with the CachyOS LTS kernel as fallback | The CachyOS ISO, or the script installer on CachyOS

This page is about the middle row: what the layer adds, how to get it, and how
to back out.

chunks.title: Kernels > Rollback
chunks.text:
- Boot the stock kernel. The stock Arch kernel is never removed. Pick its
  entry in the Limine menu and you are back.
- Recover the whole transaction. Installing the layer is a pacman
  transaction, so snapper and snap-pac take a pre and post snapshot pair and
  limine-snapper-sync lists them in the boot menu. See Updates.
- Remove it. Remove the bundle's items in Ryostore. The `[cachyos-v3]`
  repository line stays in `/etc/pacman.conf`; it is inert with no CachyOS
  packages installed, so delete it by hand only if you want a clean file.

chunks.title: Kernels > See also
chunks.text:
The installer questions, including the CachyOS layer.

Snapshots, the boot-menu recovery path, and how updates stay reversible.

chunks.title: Kernels > Should you switch?
chunks.text:
- An optimized, patched kernel with `sched-ext`, so you can try a latency
      or gaming scheduler.
    - CachyOS's system tuning and the auto-nice rules, which keep a busy
      machine responsive.
    - CachyOS Proton for games.

- Kernel updates now depend on one more upstream being healthy.
    - Every DKMS module rebuilds against the new kernel; a failed rebuild means
      that module is missing on that kernel until it is fixed.
    - The CachyOS kernel tracks mainline more closely than Arch's `linux`.

The gain is real for gamers and heavy multitaskers; a light desktop will barely
notice it.

chunks.title: Kernels > What the CachyOS layer adds
chunks.text:
- The `[cachyos-v3]` repository above `[core]`, trusted through the CachyOS
  signing key, and multilib for Proton's 32-bit libraries.
- `linux-cachyos` and `linux-cachyos-headers`: EEVDF with `sched-ext`, Clang
  ThinLTO and AutoFDO, the Cachy patchset, built for x86-64-v3.
- `cachyos-settings`: CachyOS's sysctl, udev, modprobe and systemd tuning.
- `scx-scheds`: the sched-ext userspace schedulers (bpfland, rusty, lavd).
- `ananicy-cpp` and `cachyos-ananicy-rules`: the auto-nice daemon that keeps
  the compositor and foreground apps responsive under load.
- `proton-cachyos-native`: the CachyOS Proton build for Steam and Lutris.

chunks.title: Kernels > What the CachyOS layer adds
chunks.text:
It does not add the baseline `[cachyos]` repository (CachyOS's forked
pacman) or the `cachyos-core-v3` and `cachyos-extra-v3` userland rebuilds, so a
later `pacman -Syu` cannot quietly replace your userland or your package
manager. Your desktop, defaults and the `[ryoku]` repository stay as they were.

The layer needs a CPU with x86-64-v3 support (almost every CPU since about
2015). On a CPU without it, the installer skips the layer and says why.

chunks.title: Maintenance > Branches
chunks.text:
Work goes to `unstable-dev`. Every push there runs the Testing gate, which
waits for the required checks and then records the commit for testers on
`ryoku track unstable`; the package publishers run the same gate before they
upload the testing repositories. `main` only moves by a fast-forward from
`unstable-dev` when a release is ready, and a release is the Stable Release
workflow run on `main`. See Release pipeline.

chunks.title: Maintenance > Commits
chunks.text:
Every commit passes the hooks in `.githooks/`; install them with
`bin/ryoku-dev-install-hooks`. Never use `--no-verify`.

- The subject is `[area] scope: imperative summary`, 72 characters or fewer,
  no trailing period. The area is one of `global`, `installation`, `system`,
  `ryoku`, `docs`, `test`, `tooling`, `release`.
- No em-dash anywhere, no authorship or attribution trailers, no filler.
- One logical change per commit, with the matching `CHANGELOG.md` entry.
- Anything a user would notice gets a plain-language trailer that the release
  bot collects into the release notes:

```text
Note: New: pin an app by right-clicking it in the dock
Note: Fixed: right-clicking a dock app now saves or removes the pin
Note: Removed: the old instant-replay buffer
```

chunks.title: Maintenance > How a change reaches a user
chunks.text:
A dev box runs the checkout; users run packages. Where a change lives decides
how it gets there.

Change | Vehicle
Desktop config and binaries (`ryoku/`) | Signed packages, then `ryoku materialize` re-lays the base config on the next `ryoku update`. User edits live in `~/.config/ryoku/user_edits` and survive.
A new default app or package | The edition's package set for new installs, and the provisioning manifest so existing installs receive it once. Apps a user left out stay out.
The installers (`installation/`, `ryoku-shell-installer/`) | New installs only. A change to the script installer means rebuilding its committed binary and checksum.
Stateful drift nothing above can express | An idempotent `ryoku doctor` reconciler, which runs inside every `ryoku update`.

chunks.title: Maintenance > How a change reaches a user
chunks.text:
There is no ordered migration ledger. A removed or renamed `shell.json` key
needs a doctor reconciler, and `bin/ryoku-dev-verify-delivery` checks that
every shipped config reaches users.

chunks.title: Maintenance > Overview
chunks.text:
How to work in the Ryoku repository: the
dev loop, the gates a commit passes, the path a change takes from the repo to a
user's machine, and where new code belongs.

The in-repo guides are the source of truth and override anything that drifts
here: `AGENTS.md`,
`CONTRIBUTING.md`,
`docs/development.md`
and `docs/updates.md`.

chunks.text:

  signed repositories.

chunks.title: Maintenance > The dev loop
chunks.text:
Ryoku is developed on a running Ryoku machine. Edit the repo, deploy, test on
the running system. Never edit `~/.config` directly and copy it back; the flow
is repo to system only.

```bash
ryoku/shell/dev-run.sh       # build ryoku-shell and run it from the checkout (hot reload)
ryoku/shell/dev-binds.sh on  # bind the shell keys to the dev shell for this session
ryoku/shell/dev-stop.sh      # stop the dev shell
ryoku/shell/deploy.sh        # lay the repo into ~/.config and rebuild the binaries
```

`dev-run.sh` leaves your own `~/.config` alone. On an installed system the same
config arrives through `ryoku materialize`, which lays the base config in from
the packages; the `ryoku` command detects which world it is in.

chunks.title: Maintenance > Verify before committing
chunks.text:
Test behavior on the running system, not only that a file parses:

- Lua: `luac -p `.
- Shell scripts: `bash -n `; `shellcheck` runs on push.
- QML: `qmllint`, and `bin/ryoku-dev-lint-qml` on a dev box.
- Go: `go build ./... && go vet ./... && go test ./...` in each module you
  touched.
- Installer: run the backend with `RYOKU_DRYRUN=1` to print every action
  without touching a disk.
- The seam and delivery: `bin/ryoku-dev-verify-wm-isolation` and
  `bin/ryoku-dev-verify-delivery`.

chunks.title: Maintenance > Where new code goes
chunks.text: Intent | Where it goes A package every machine should have | The matching set in `system/packages/`, plus its rows in the Void and Fedora translation tables. Prefer official repositories over the AUR. A keybind | The neutral catalogue in `ryoku/wm/binds.go`; each compositor provider renders it. A compositor concern | That compositor's own config: Lua modules under `ryoku/hyprland/`, KDL under `ryoku/niri/`. Nothing outside `ryoku/wm/` names a compositor; the desktop asks capabilities. A shell surface | A component under `ryoku/shell/quickshell/`, with its state wired through `ryoku-shell` (`ryoku/shell/ipc/`). QML renders; the Go daemon decides. A Ryoku Settings page or control | The Hub under `ryoku/hub/`, with the logic in its Go backend. A doctor reconciler | A file under `ryoku/cli/internal/doctor/`, registered in its list. Idempotent, cheap to check, safe to repeat. A new app's

chunks.text: native config | `ryoku/apps//` in the tool's own format. Never a Lua wrapper for a tool that reads its own config. A new `[ryoku]` package | `release/packages//`, with its Fedora spec and Void template beside the other editions' builds.

chunks.title: Maintenance > Writing prose
chunks.text:
- No em-dash. Use a comma, a colon, a period or parentheses.
- No emoji, no marketing fluff. Plain, direct, technical prose.
- Match the files next to yours. When in doubt, copy the closest neighbour.
- Comment the *why* when it is not obvious. Never narrate the *what* or
  leave commented-out code.

chunks.title: Navigation > Float and fullscreen
chunks.text:
- `Mod + F` toggles fullscreen for the active window.
- `Mod + A` floats the active window, centred. Press it again to tile it back
  into the layout. Reach for it when you want a calculator, a small dialog, or
  one window lifted out of the tiles.
- `Mod + D` fills the screen width while keeping the gaps and the bar, and
  `Mod + C` centres the window.

chunks.title: Navigation > Focus and move windows
chunks.text:
Focus follows direction, not a fixed cycle order.

Press | Does
`Mod + Arrow` | Move focus to the neighbour in that direction.
`Mod + Shift + Arrow` | Move the active window in that direction.

`Alt + Tab` jumps back to the previously focused window. To jump straight to a
specific window, open the launcher (`Mod + Space`) and type its title or app
name: the launcher lists open windows alongside apps and focuses the one you
pick. The overview (`Mod + Tab`) is the visual alternative:
click any window to focus it.

chunks.title: Navigation > Mouse
chunks.text:
You rarely need the mouse, but it is there when a quick drag is faster:

- `Mod + Left-drag` moves the window under the cursor.
- `Mod + Right-drag` resizes it.

chunks.title: Navigation > Multiple monitors
chunks.text:
Ryoku is monitor-aware. Because `Mod + 1 … 0` pulls the target workspace to the
monitor your cursor is on, the workspace keys always act on the screen you are
pointing at, so you never reach for a different set of binds per display.

`Mod + Alt + Arrow` focuses the screen in that direction, and adding `Shift`
sends the active window there. `Mod + P` cycles the displays through internal
only, external only and both. Set resolutions, scale, rotation and layout on
the Displays page of Settings; see
Hardware for the details.
