chunks.text:
Every shipped bind in one reference table.

The shell surfaces you are navigating between.

chunks.title: Navigation > Open a couple of windows
chunks.text:
When you log in nothing is open, because a tiling window manager only shows
what you launch. Open one window, then a second, and watch the screen split
between them.

`Mod + Return` opens the terminal (`kitty`). It fills the whole work area,
    because it is the only window.

`Mod + B` opens your browser (Firefox unless you picked another). It tiles
    in next to the terminal, each taking half the screen. Every new window
    slots into the current layout the same way.

`Mod + Q` closes the active window. The launcher (`Mod + Space`) opens anything
else: type to filter, `Enter` to launch.

chunks.title: Navigation > Overview
chunks.text:
Hyprland and niri are tiling window managers. New windows claim their share of
the screen automatically: no dragging, no overlapping stacks to shuffle. You
drive the whole desktop from the keyboard, and `Mod` is `Super` (the Windows or
Cmd key). Some details below differ on niri, which scrolls windows in columns;
Kit (`Mod + K`) lists the exact keys for the window manager you run.

This page walks the everyday workflow. Keybindings is the
exhaustive reference for every shipped bind; come back here for how they fit
together.

chunks.title: Navigation > Resize windows
chunks.text:
Two ways, depending on whether you want a quick nudge or a sustained resize.

- Nudge. `Mod + Ctrl + Arrow` grows or shrinks the active window a step at a
  time. Hold it to keep resizing.
- Resize mode. `Mod + R` enters resize mode. Now the bare arrows (or
  `hjkl`) resize the window, and `Esc` leaves the mode.

chunks.title: Navigation > Scratchpad
chunks.text:
The scratchpad is a hidden workspace for a window you want one keypress away,
such as a notes terminal, a chat or a music player.

- `Mod + H` tucks the active window into the scratchpad. Press it again on that
  window to bring it back.
- `Mod + Alt + H` shows or hides the scratchpad.

chunks.title: Navigation > The overview
chunks.text:
`Mod + Tab` opens a full-screen expo: every workspace on the current desktop as
a scaled mini-desktop with live window previews. From here you can:

- Click a workspace to switch to it, or click a window to focus it.
- Drag a window between workspaces, or up onto the top strip to move it to
  another desktop.
- Hover a window for a `✕` to close it.
- Scroll or `Tab` to move the selection, `Enter` to commit, `Esc` to dismiss.

A second level shows your desktops, each a block of ten workspaces with its
own 01–10 set, so you can keep separate groups of workspaces for different work.
`Mod + Alt + Tab` steps between desktops (`Tab` again inside the overview cycles
them).

chunks.title: Navigation > Workspaces
chunks.text:
Each monitor carries ten workspaces.

Press | Does
`Mod + 1 … 0` | Focus workspace N on the monitor under the cursor.
`Mod + Alt + 1 … 0` | Send the active window to workspace N and follow it.
`Mod + Shift + 1 … 0` | Send the active window to workspace N and stay here.
`Mod + Scroll` | Cycle to the previous / next workspace.
`Mod + Tab` | Open the overview (workspace expo).

The number keys are desktop-relative. A *desktop* is a block of ten
workspace ids, so on desktop 2, `Mod + 3` focuses workspace 13, never
workspace 3. Each desktop keeps its own 1–10 and windows never jump between
desktops. The workspace is also pulled to whichever monitor the cursor is on,
so the same keys drive every screen instead of always yanking focus to the
laptop panel.

chunks.title: Plugins > A bar panel
chunks.text:
A bar widget is more than a mark. Its glyph on the bar shows a glance of state;
click it and a panel opens beneath it, in the same surface the shell's own
panels use, closing on `Escape` or an outside click. The widget declares one
extra view and a width, and Ryoku draws and sizes the panel for it, capped to
your screen. Clicking the bar only ever *opens* the panel; it never changes
anything on its own. The actions live inside the panel, behind buttons you press.

The VPN plugin in Ryostore is the worked example: its glyph shows whether a VPN
is up, and its panel holds the switch, the connection details, and an AUTHORISE
button that asks for your password once.

chunks.title: Plugins > Ask Rashin for one
chunks.text:
You do not have to write a widget by hand. If Rashin is on,
describe the bar widget you want and its agent builds it, installs it with
`ryoku plugin add`, and drops it into Community for you to review. See
Asking for a widget.

chunks.title: Plugins > Bar widgets from the community
chunks.text:
The catalogue's official plugins are only half the picture. Anyone can write a
bar widget and share it, and the ones you add yourself live in QS Bar Settings
Community. Open that panel from the bar's logo, from `Mod + Escape` then
QS Bar, or with:

```bash
ryoku-shell bar settings community
```

Community lists each plugin you added, with its author, a switch, its own
settings, and EXPORT, SHARE TO RYOSTORE, and REMOVE buttons. It opens
on a warning that applies to all of them:

Community plugin. Ryoku does not review or maintain it: it runs inside your
  shell with your permissions, so inspect its code before you trust it.

To add one, paste a git URL or a local folder into the panel's ADD field, or
run:

```bash
ryoku plugin add  --bar
```

chunks.title: Plugins > Bar widgets from the community
chunks.text:
Either way Ryoku validates the plugin, installs it through Ryostore's
transaction (a receipt and a content-hashed copy), places it on the bar, and the
shell picks it up within seconds, no restart. Remove it with the REMOVE
button or:

```bash
ryoku plugin remove
```

chunks.title: Plugins > Make one
chunks.text:
You do not start from a blank folder. One command scaffolds a complete, working
plugin in the right place:

```bash
ryoku plugin new my-widget --bar
```

That writes `~/Documents/ryoku-plugins/my-widget/` with a template you can run

`ryoku plugin new ` creates the folder and fills it with a template that

Change the logic, the view, and (for a bar widget) the panel; write the

`ryoku plugin validate ` runs the safety checks and tells you, line by

Find it on the bar and under QS Bar Settings > Community. When you want
    to publish it, and only then, `ryoku plugin share ` opens the Ryostore

chunks.title: Plugins > Overview
chunks.text:
A plugin is a small widget you place on your desktop: a stock ticker on
the wallpaper, a photo beside the clock, a panel that melts out of the screen
edge on hover. The author writes the *logic and one view*; Ryoku owns *where it
lives, how it looks, how it moves, and how it sizes*. That split is the whole
point, a plugin always looks and behaves like a native part of the shell,
because the shell draws the surface around it.

Plugins are widgets, not applications. To install real software (game
  launchers, dev stacks, VPN clients), use Extras bundles, a
  separate system.

chunks.title: Plugins > Remove a plugin's files (your placement in plugins.json is kept).
chunks.text: ryostore remove plugins market

chunks.title: Plugins > See also
chunks.text:
Software bundles, the other half of how Ryoku grows beyond its core.

The Add-ons page, and everything else the Hub tunes.

chunks.title: Plugins > Share a widget you made
chunks.text:
Made something worth passing on? Turn an installed plugin into a shareable folder
with:

```bash
ryoku plugin export
```

That writes `~/Documents/ryoku-plugins//` (or `~/ryoku-plugins/` if you
have no Documents directory) and puts it under git. Inside are the plugin's files
plus two Ryostore descriptors: `product-manifest.json` (the per-file checksums
Ryostore verifies against) and `registry-entry.json` (the catalogue entry,
marked `official: false`).

When you are ready to publish, run:

```bash
ryoku plugin share
```

With the GitHub CLI (`gh`) logged in this opens a pull request against Ryostore;
without it, it opens the submission form prefilled. A maintainer then reviews the
entry before it appears in the catalogue.

chunks.title: Plugins > Share a widget you made
chunks.text:
Ryostore review is a listing review, whether the entry belongs in the
  catalogue and is described honestly, not a security audit. Nobody vets the
  code for you, which is why every community plugin keeps the warning above. Read
  the source before you install one.

chunks.title: Plugins > The catalogue
chunks.text:
Ryostore carries more than fifty plugins, among them:

Track any Yahoo Finance symbol, a crypto pair (`BTC-USD`), a stock (`AAPL`),
    or an index (`^GSPC`), with live price, change, and history in one of four
    faces: dossier, line, area, or minimal.

Pin any photo to your wallpaper in a chosen style (rounded, square, polaroid,
    framed, or film) with a tunable drop shadow and colour filters.

Clock, calendar, weather, media, notes, to-dos, system resources and more,
    ported from end4's illogical-impulse. The MJ Widget Set bundle installs
    all 25 at once.

An analog clock, audio, media, screen time and a dashboard in the Nothing
    style.

Each plugin's own options (Market's symbol and face, Photo Frame's style and
filter) live in its settings, edited from the Add-ons page or the desktop
widget's right-click menu.

chunks.title: Plugins > The hosts
chunks.text:
When you enable a plugin you pick one host for it. The same widget can run in
any host its manifest declares; Ryoku just renders it differently.

A tile on the wallpaper, next to the clock and calendar, with the same
    machinery they have:

- Left-drag to move it (snaps to a grid).

chunks.title: Plugins > The rules
chunks.text:
A plugin runs inside your shell with your permissions, so a good one plays by a
few plain rules. `ryoku plugin validate` checks the ones it can, and Ryostore
runs the same check on anything submitted:

chunks.title: Plugins > The rules
chunks.text: - Stay in your folder. A plugin is one folder named after its id; it never writes into the shell's own config or the store's install folder. - Ship the standard pieces. A manifest, the logic, one view, an optional bar panel, a README, a LICENSE, and a real preview image. Scripts live in `bin/`. - Import only the kit. Views use Ryoku's PluginKit and Qt, never the shell's private internals, so a shell update never breaks them. - Settings go through the manifest. You declare them; the shell draws and saves them. A plugin never edits the shell's settings files by hand. - Be honest about programs. Every command a plugin runs is shipped with it or listed in the manifest. No `sudo`; anything that needs a password uses the system prompt (`pkexec`), only on a click you make, and says so in the README. - Be honest about the network. Every server a plugin talks to is listed in the manifest. Nothing

chunks.title: Plugins > The rules
chunks.text:
downloads and runs more code. - Write only your own scratch space. A plugin writes to its own state and cache folders, never to your `~/.ssh`, your system files, or another plugin. - No hidden code. No secrets in the files, no compiled binaries, no symlinks; just readable scripts and QML. - Tell the truth. A community plugin is marked community, names its author, and its README says what it runs, reads, writes, and asks for.

The full rule list, with the exact wording the validator uses, is in the
authoring guide.

chunks.title: Plugins > Uninstall a plugin and drop its placement.
chunks.text:
ryoku plugin remove
```

chunks.title: Plugins > Write your own
chunks.text:
Yes, Ryoku has a plugin SDK. A plugin is a folder with a `manifest.json`, a
non-visual `service/Main.qml` (your logic and state), and one `content/Widget.qml`
(your view), installed to `~/.local/share/ryoku/plugins//`. Your view imports
the `Ryoku.PluginKit` deck kit, so it picks up the shell's colours, type, and
motion automatically.

The golden rule: never set your own position, never draw your own window
  chrome, never assume your size. You report your content's natural
  `implicitWidth` and `implicitHeight`; Ryoku sizes the card or grows the popout
  around it. Break this rule and your plugin looks bolted-on instead of native.

The full authoring guide, the manifest schema, the three densities (`glyph`,
`compact`, `full`), and the settings schema live in the repo:

chunks.title: Plugins > Write your own
chunks.text:
- `docs/plugins.md` in the Ryoku repo, the canonical guide.
- `plugins/AUTHORING.md` in `ryostore`, alongside a `template/` plugin to copy.

chunks.title: Rashin > Asking for a widget
chunks.text:
Rashin's agent knows the bar, so you can describe a bar widget in plain words
instead of writing one. Ask from the dashboard's Chat, the `\` launcher, or
`ryoku-rashin chat "..."`; all reach Hermes with the `ryoku` skill wired in. What
it does depends on what you ask:

You say | What Rashin does
"Make me a VPN widget for my bar that shows whether my VPN is up and lets me toggle it" | Writes a plugin folder (manifest, service, and view) and installs it with `ryoku plugin add  --bar`.
"Move the clock to the right of the bar" | Runs `ryoku-shell bar ...` to rearrange the widgets already on the bar.
"Hide the memory widget and show GPU instead" | Runs `ryoku-shell bar ...` to toggle which built-in widgets show.

chunks.title: Rashin > Asking for a widget
chunks.text:
A widget it builds lands in QS Bar Settings > Community, the same place a
hand-installed one does (see [Bar widgets from the
community](/docs/plugins#bar-widgets-from-the-community)). It runs with your
permissions, so read the code, tweak it, and only then [share
it](/docs/plugins#share-a-widget-you-made). Rearrangements take effect on the bar
right away.

To build against the real desktop, the agent reads its `ryoku` skill (`bar.md`
for the QS Bar and `plugins.md`, the widget contract) and the vault's
`desktop.md`, so it knows the host to target and where the bar's
config lives.

chunks.title: Rashin > In the installer
chunks.text:
The installers ask about Rashin with a short explanation, and the answer
defaults to yes:

- Yes installs `ryoku-rashin`. Rashin runs the Hermes agent as its harness,
  and Hermes installs at your first login: once the machine is online, a
  terminal opens and runs the setup below. Offline, it waits for a later login.
- No leaves `ryoku-rashin` out and records that, so updates never install
  it. The Ask and Rashin shortcuts are not registered while it is absent.

chunks.title: Rashin > Overview
chunks.text:
Rashin (羅針, "compass needle") is Ryoku's AI agent. It answers quick questions
in the Ask bar (`Alt + Space`), does longer work in Agent mode and the Rashin
window (`Super + Alt + Space`), shows your AI usage in the bar, and maintains a
map of your machine, a knowledge vault, that any coding agent can read instead
of rediscovering your system. Everything it does stays on your machine.

Three pieces make it up:

- A knowledge vault of generated markdown maps (your hardware, your desktop
  config, your packages, your own changes) that agents read and write.
- A local dashboard on `127.0.0.1` with vitals, the vault, and a chat
  surface.
- One-click setup for Hermes, the resident agent, wired to the vault.

chunks.title: Rashin > Privacy
chunks.text:
Rashin is built to keep everything local:

- Loopback only. The daemon binds `127.0.0.1`, and WebSocket connections are
  rejected unless their origin is localhost. No listener leaves your machine.
- Nothing leaves the machine on its own. The vault is markdown on your disk;
  Rashin does not phone home.
- You bring your own model. Rashin bundles no LLM. Hermes uses the provider
  and model you choose during setup, so where prompts go is your choice.
- Off until you set it up. The gate in `~/.config/ryoku/rashin.json` is the
  single source of truth; a disabled Rashin does nothing even if its service
  fires.

For how Rashin fits Ryoku's wider security posture (signed releases,
snapshots and disk encryption), see Security.

chunks.title: Rashin > Quick asks
chunks.text:
You do not have to open the dashboard to ask a question. Two surfaces share the
same brain (the daemon, the vault, and your Hermes connection):

Open the launcher with `Mod + Space`, type `\`, then your question. The
    answer streams back with action chips: open a file, jump to a directory,
    open a link, or copy a command or color. Type `\resume` to recall a recent
    ask instantly, with no model call.

Run `rashin ` in the terminal. It answers from the same brain
    and drops a ready-to-run command on your prompt; you press Enter to run
    it. `rashin` never runs anything itself; the buffer is the confirmation. Every
    proposed command also carries a danger tier (read / write / system / danger).

chunks.title: Rashin > Quick asks
chunks.text:
Both lanes write to one shared history, so an ask started in the launcher can be
continued in the dashboard, and `\resume` in the launcher and `rashin --resume`
in the terminal see the same conversation.

remote listener. It is a self-contained page with a distinct Japanese
retro-poster look, deliberately separate from the desktop theme.

Panel | What it shows
Overview | Live vitals, daemon and Hermes state, code-intelligence stats
Vault | Browse and read the generated maps; reindex on demand
Memory | Agent memory, a graph of notes, and session history
Skills | Every Hermes skill and the enabled toolbelt
Agents | Detected coding CLIs and their wiring state

chunks.title: Rashin > The vault
chunks.text:
The vault is the shared knowledge base every agent reads and writes, at
`~/.local/share/ryoku/rashin/`. Ryoku generates the maps; you and your agents own
the notes.

File | What it holds
`AGENTS.md` | The entry contract agents read first (`CLAUDE.md` is a symlink to it)
`system.md` | Hardware, kernel, drivers, displays
`desktop.md` | The Ryoku map: where every config lives, what owns it, how to reload it
`packages.md` | Package sets, versions, and update state
`user.md` | Where your config diverges from the shipped defaults
`habits.md` | Your directories, tool stack, and shell rhythms
`memory/` and `journal/` | Agent-writable notes and dated entries

chunks.title: Rashin > The vault
chunks.text:
The generated files stay current on their own: Rashin reindexes on daemon start,
on a timer, from the dashboard's reindex button, and after every `ryoku update`,
so agents always see the system as it is now. Only the generated content is
rewritten; anything you or an agent adds around it survives.

Because the vault is plain markdown, it works with the coding agents you already
use. When Rashin wires an agent (Claude Code, Codex, opencode, Oh My Pi, Hermes),
it points that agent at `AGENTS.md` so it reads the map before guessing paths.

chunks.title: Rashin > Turn it on or off later
chunks.text:
Press `Mod + ,` to open Ryoku Settings, then open the
    Rashin page. The master switch installs or removes Rashin.

Set up Hermes agent runs the setup in a floating terminal (never with
    `sudo`). It installs Hermes if it is not already present, runs Hermes's
    onboarding so you pick your own provider and model, wires the vault so
    agents read it, and enables the daemon. The same setup runs from a
    terminal with `ryoku-rashin setup`.

When setup finishes it opens the dashboard at
    http://127.0.0.1:3600. From then on the daemon
    starts at login and keeps the vault current.

If you already run Hermes, setup leaves it alone: it skips install and
onboarding and only wires the vault, so your provider and model choices are
untouched. The script installer also skips the first-login setup when it finds
Hermes already installed.

chunks.title: Security > Local-only Rashin
chunks.text:
Ryoku's agent, Rashin, keeps everything on your machine: its daemon binds
`127.0.0.1` only, rejects non-localhost WebSocket origins, and bundles no model
of its own, so you choose the provider. The knowledge vault it builds is plain
markdown on your disk, and you can leave Rashin out in the installer. See
Rashin for the full picture.

Security-sensitive issues follow the project's `SECURITY.md`, not the public
issue tracker.

chunks.title: Security > Overview
chunks.text:
Ryoku's security model is boring on purpose: everything you install is signed and
verifiable, every update is reversible, and nothing on the machine talks to the
network unless you tell it to. This page collects the guarantees and the exact
commands to check them.

chunks.title: Security > Repo trust
chunks.text:
The installer adds the `[ryoku]` repo and imports the release key from the
`ryoku-keyring` package, which ships the key material into pacman's keyring. From
then on pacman verifies the signature on every `[ryoku]` package it installs or
upgrades, so `ryoku update` only ever applies signed packages. You never have to
re-import the key by hand. See Updates for where the packages
come from.

chunks.title: Security > See also
chunks.text:
Verify and boot a signed ISO, and choose disk encryption.

Signed packages, snapshots, and rollback.

chunks.title: Security > Show the fingerprint and compare it against the one above
chunks.text: gpg --fingerprint releases@ryoku.dev

chunks.title: Security > Signed releases
chunks.text:
Every Ryoku ISO and every package in the Ryoku repositories (pacman, XBPS and
RPM) is signed by the release identity `Ryoku Releases `.
The canonical public key lives in the repo at
`keys/ryoku-release-key.pub.asc`,
bound to git history, and ships alongside each ISO.

The key fingerprint to verify against is:

```
EB6D3C0F55A7B3CABA6B2838847B274F025DD6E3
```

Always compare the imported key's fingerprint against the value above before you
trust it. A signature only means something once you have confirmed the key that
made it is the real release key.

chunks.title: Security > Snapshots as a safety net
chunks.text:
On a standard install (a btrfs root with snapper configured, which the ISO sets
up) every `ryoku update` is wrapped in a pre/post snapshot pair. A bad update is
never a dead end: roll back with `ryoku rollback`, and if the desktop will not
come up, the same snapshots are selectable straight from the Limine boot menu.
The full model (prerequisites, self-healing and recovery) is in
Updates.

chunks.title: Security > Verify the ISO against its detached signature and its checksum
chunks.text:
gpg --verify ryoku--x86_64.iso.sig ryoku--x86_64.iso
sha256sum -c ryoku--x86_64.iso.sha256
```

`gpg --verify` must report a good signature from the release identity, and
`sha256sum -c` must print `OK`. If either fails, do not boot the image. The full
walkthrough of what good output looks like is in [Install](/docs/install).

focusing, moving and tiling windows) see Navigation; to

The full-screen workspace expo (`Mod +

chunks.title: Desktop tour > Shell surfaces
chunks.text:
The Go daemon (`ryoku-shell`, in `ryoku/shell/ipc/`) is the control plane: it
supervises the persistent components and decides what is on screen, and the QML
frontend renders it. Theme tokens flow from the wallpaper through `matugen`, so
picking a new wallpaper repaints every surface without restarting anything.

chunks.title: Desktop tour > The shell daemon's log (Arch, CachyOS and Fedora)
chunks.text: journalctl --user -u ryoku-shell -f

chunks.title: Desktop tour > What the window manager reports
chunks.text:
ryoku wm status
```

`ryoku-shell` runs as a user service that starts with your session;
`ryoku reload` restarts it.

chunks.title: Desktop tour > Where things live
chunks.text:
Thing | Hyprland | niri
Entry point | `~/.config/hypr/hyprland.lua` | `~/.config/niri/config.kdl`
Your overrides (loaded last, always win) | `~/.config/hypr/user.lua` | `~/.config/niri/user.kdl`
Manual monitor pinning | `~/.config/hypr/monitors_user.lua` | `~/.config/niri/monitors_user.kdl`
Generated displays and GPU | `monitors.lua`, `gpu.lua` | `monitors.kdl`, `gpu.kdl`
What Ryoku Settings writes | `settings.lua` | `settings.kdl`, `rebinds.kdl`

Your Ryoku Settings changes are kept in `~/.config/ryoku/user_edits`.
Wallpapers live in `~/Pictures/Wallpapers`, and per-app overrides such as
`~/.config/kitty/user.conf` and `~/.config/fish/user.fish` are left alone by
updates. Customize covers what to put in each layer.

chunks.title: Troubleshoot > A read-only state check
chunks.text:
`ryoku status` answers "is this machine current and healthy?" without
touching anything. It reports the active config base, the installed
`ryoku-desktop` version, what the `[ryoku]` repo offers, the count of pending
updates, and the snapshot count.

```bash
ryoku status
```

chunks.title: Troubleshoot > Filing a useful bug
chunks.text:
Open an issue at
github.com/Ryoku-dev/ryoku/issues
with:

1. What you did: keystrokes, clicks, or commands.
2. What happened: what you saw, including screenshots when relevant.
3. What you expected.
4. The output of `ryoku status` and a fresh `ryoku doctor --report`. Attach
   `~/.local/state/ryoku/doctor-report.txt` directly; it has no secrets in
   it.
5. The relevant log slice. The last 50 lines of
   `~/.local/state/ryoku-shell.log` (after a `ryoku reload`) is usually
   enough for shell issues.

Security-sensitive issues follow the project's `SECURITY.md`, not the public
tracker.

chunks.title: Troubleshoot > No snapshots, or `ryoku snapshots` says the config 'root' does not exist
chunks.text:
`ryoku snapshots` printing `The config 'root' does not exist. Likely snapper
is not configured.`, an empty Limine snapshot menu, or `ryoku status`
reporting zero snapshots after several updates all point to the same thing:
the snapper `root` config is missing, so the safety net never ran. Snapshots
require a btrfs root; the standard ISO install sets the config up
automatically, but a machine that skipped the installer step, was upgraded
from an older install, or drifted can end up without it.

First, confirm the root is btrfs:

```bash
findmnt -no FSTYPE /
```

If that prints `btrfs`, run `ryoku doctor`. The snapper reconciler creates
`/etc/snapper/configs/root` from the same template the installer uses,
registers it in `/etc/conf.d/snapper`, fixes `/.snapshots` ownership, and
enables the cleanup timer:

```bash
ryoku doctor
ryoku snapshots
ryoku status
```

chunks.title: Troubleshoot > No snapshots, or `ryoku snapshots` says the config 'root' does not exist
chunks.text:
The next `ryoku update` then writes a pre/post snapshot pair like any other
run.

If `findmnt` prints anything other than `btrfs`, the snapshot feature is
unavailable on this machine and `ryoku update` will keep proceeding without
snapshots. Rollback from inside Ryoku is not possible there; use your own
backup or a reinstall instead.

chunks.title: Troubleshoot > Only one resolution, or a display change will not apply
chunks.text:
Laptop (eDP) panels expose only their native resolution; use the scale
options instead. They are labelled with the logical resolution they produce
(for example 2048x1280) and are the Wayland way to get a smaller desktop. If
`Apply` toasts a rejection, the compositor refused that mode or scale; pick
one of the offered clean-divisor scales.

chunks.title: Troubleshoot > Overview
chunks.text:
When something goes wrong, work in this order: read the logs, run
`ryoku doctor`, roll back a bad update with `ryoku rollback`, and only then
file a bug. The same `ryoku` CLI that updates the machine also surfaces every
diagnostic you need.

This page is the problem-first path through the `ryoku` CLI; the
CLI reference documents every command it uses in full.

chunks.title: Troubleshoot > Performance feels off
chunks.text:
- Animations: the Animations page in Ryoku Settings turns them down or
  off.
- Wallpaper: turning off animated or video wallpapers is the single biggest
  GPU win.
- Blur and shadows: the Performance page trades eye candy for lower CPU,
  GPU and memory use, and can follow the power profile so Power Saver strips
  blur and shadows on its own.

chunks.title: Troubleshoot > Recover a bad update: `ryoku rollback`
chunks.text:
Every `ryoku update` is wrapped in a snapper pre/post snapshot pair. If an
update breaks the system, roll back:

```bash
ryoku snapshots
ryoku rollback 42
```

With no id, `ryoku rollback` lists snapshots so you can pick one. The same
snapshots are selectable from the Limine boot menu, so a system that will
not boot back into Hyprland can be recovered from the bootloader instead.

If you cannot reach the desktop at all, drop to a TTY (`Ctrl+Alt+F2`), log
in, and run `ryoku rollback` from there.

chunks.title: Troubleshoot > See also
chunks.text:
- Updates for the snapshot model and rollback details.
- Customize for the override files that update-safely
  survive every run.
- Keybindings for the shortcuts that open Settings,
  reload the shell, and pick a wallpaper.
- CLI for the full `ryoku` command reference.
- FAQ for quick answers to common problems.

chunks.title: Troubleshoot > Self-heal first: `ryoku doctor`
chunks.text:
`ryoku doctor` runs idempotent reconcilers for the stateful drift the package
and config layers cannot express. Each reconciler reports `ok` when the
machine matches the desired state, otherwise it converges, proposes the exact
fix, or flags it for a human. A healthy machine is quiet.

```bash
ryoku doctor --check
```

`--check` (or `-n`) shows the full list without changing anything. Run it
first to see what doctor would do.

To collect a report for a maintainer or for yourself, bundle the findings
with system state (btrfs, swap, failed units, recent journal errors, pacman
state, the ryoku channel state, display and backlight):

```bash
ryoku doctor --report
```

The report is written to `~/.local/state/ryoku/doctor-report.txt`; it
contains no passwords or keys.

chunks.title: Troubleshoot > Self-heal first: `ryoku doctor`
chunks.text:
When you want it to reason rather than match rules, `ryoku doctor --explain`
sends that same report to a cloud model for a root-cause analysis and fix
steps. It is opt-in, advisory and read-only: it never runs anything, so a wrong
answer can only mislead, and it uses your own key. See CLI for
configuring the key and the provider endpoint.

The reconciler set is broad (the stateful drift a Ryoku machine accumulates
across snapshots, packages, session components and the generated compositor
config) and it grows over time, so the current list lives in CLI.
When something specific breaks, `ryoku doctor --check` tells you whether a
reconciler already handles it.

chunks.title: Troubleshoot > The installer won't advance past "Disk layout"
chunks.text:
Installing alongside Windows and pressing Tab on the Disk layout step
does nothing? The alongside layout is blocked, and the screen shows a red `⚠`
with the reason. Usually there is no free space and no partition selected to
shrink: select one and use `←`/`→` to give Ryoku room, or shrink Windows
yourself first. A hibernated Windows volume (Fast Startup on) cannot be shrunk
safely. The full walkthrough is in Dual-boot with Windows.
On a dedicated drive, press `esc` and choose Erase whole disk instead.

chunks.title: Troubleshoot > The last-resort recovery
chunks.text:
When the desktop is too broken to update normally (a corrupt local config, a
broken local build), `ryoku recovery` resets to `main` and redeploys,
overwriting configs. It hands off to `bin/ryoku-recovery`, preferring a local
copy and otherwise fetching the canonical script over the network, so it
still works when the local install is broken.

```bash
ryoku recovery
```

chunks.title: Troubleshoot > The login screen is broken
chunks.text:
If SDDM does not start or refuses logins, drop to a TTY (`Ctrl+Alt+F2`), log
in, and start Hyprland directly:

```bash
Hyprland
```

If Hyprland starts fine from the TTY, SDDM is the problem; read its log:

```bash
sudo journalctl -u sddm -n 200
```

Switch the SDDM theme from Ryoku Settings > Lockscreen and Login if you
can reach a desktop, or edit `/etc/sddm.conf.d/` directly.

chunks.title: Troubleshoot > The shell or bar is not drawing
chunks.text:
If the bar, sidebar, or other shell surfaces are missing:

```bash
ryoku reload
tail -n 100 ~/.local/state/ryoku-shell.log
```

The common causes:

- A recent `ryoku update` left the shell out of sync. Run `ryoku update`
  again; if that fails, `ryoku rollback` to the pre-update snapshot.
- A hand-edited `~/.config/hypr/user.lua` or `~/.config/hypr/monitors_user.lua`
  has a Lua error. `pcall` keeps the rest of the config alive, but you will
  see the failure in `~/.local/state/ryoku-shell.log` and in
  `hyprctl monitors`. Comment out the line and `ryoku reload`.
- `monitors.lua` or `gpu.lua` got corrupted on a hotplug or GPU reset.
  `ryoku doctor` repairs both; if you can reach a TTY, run it there and
  log back in.

chunks.title: Troubleshoot > The wrong GPU is being used
chunks.text:
`Ryoku Settings > Displays > GPU` lists every detected GPU and pins the
primary render device through `ryoku-gpu`. On a laptop the integrated GPU is
the battery-friendly default; pick the discrete or external GPU there to
render the desktop on it. The pin is read at login, so log out and back in
to apply it.

From a terminal:

```bash
ryoku-gpu detect
```

prints what was detected and what was recommended.

chunks.title: Troubleshoot > Where logs live
chunks.text:
What | Where
Ryoku shell (bar, sidebar, panels) | `~/.local/state/ryoku-shell.log` (written when `ryoku` (re)starts the daemon)
Hyprland (the compositor) | `hyprctl monitors`, `hyprctl clients`, `dmesg`
SDDM (the login screen) | `sudo journalctl -u sddm`
Kernel and hardware | `dmesg`, `journalctl -k`
Update progress (the run) | `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/ryoku-update.json`
Doctor report (most recent) | `~/.local/state/ryoku/doctor-report.txt`

For shell issues, restart the shell to refresh its log, then read it:

```bash
ryoku reload
tail -n 50 ~/.local/state/ryoku-shell.log
hyprctl binds
```

chunks.title: Updates > Channels
chunks.text:
Channel | What it follows
**stable** | named releases, as signed packages (the default)
**unstable** | the `unstable-dev` branch, fast-forwarded to the last commit the Testing gate passed

`ryoku track unstable` moves a box to the unstable channel and
`ryoku track stable` brings it back. `ryoku track ` pins one frozen
release or unstable build, and `ryoku rollback --to ` moves the Ryoku
package set to one without a reboot.

chunks.title: Updates > Overview
chunks.text:
Ryoku updates through one command, `ryoku update`, or Update now on
Ryoku Settings > Updates. It brings the Ryoku packages current from the
signed Ryoku repository for your edition (pacman, XBPS or RPM), re-lays the base
config with `ryoku materialize`, runs `ryoku doctor`, and reloads the shell.
When the system meets the snapshot prerequisites, the run is wrapped in a
snapper pre and post snapshot.

This page covers the update and snapshot model. The full `ryoku` command
reference (every flag for `update`, `status`, `track`, `snapshots`, `rollback`,
`doctor` and `recovery`) lives in CLI.

chunks.title: Updates > Recovery
chunks.text:
When the desktop is too broken to update normally (a half-applied upgrade, a
corrupt config, a broken local build), `ryoku recovery` is the last resort. It
always restores the stable channel: it pulls `main`, reinstalls the base
packages and redeploys the desktop, overwriting Ryoku's configs. It hands off to
`bin/ryoku-recovery`, preferring a local copy and otherwise fetching the
canonical script over the network, so it still works when the local install is
broken.

```bash
ryoku recovery
```

If even the graphical session is gone, drop to a TTY (`Ctrl+Alt+F2`), log in,
and run `ryoku rollback` or `ryoku recovery` from there. The Limine boot menu
offers the same snapper snapshots if the disk itself still boots.

chunks.text:

- CLI for the full `ryoku` command reference.

chunks.title: Updates > Self-healing: `ryoku doctor`
chunks.text:
`ryoku doctor` runs idempotent reconcilers for the stateful drift that packages
and config cannot express. A healthy machine is quiet. It runs inside every
`ryoku update`, so you rarely call it by hand; `ryoku doctor --check` previews
what it would change without touching anything.

```bash
ryoku doctor --check
```

For the full reconciler set and every doctor flag (`--check`, `--report`, and
the opt-in, read-only `--explain`), see CLI. To lean on doctor
while chasing a specific problem, see Troubleshoot.

chunks.title: Updates > Snapshots and rollback
chunks.text:
When the system meets the prerequisites, every `ryoku update` is wrapped in a
snapper pre/post snapshot pair. The prerequisites are a btrfs root with a
snapper `root` config that writes snapshots to the `@snapshots` subvolume at
`/.snapshots`. The standard ISO install sets all of this up, so on a normal
install the safety net is on from first boot.

chunks.title: Updates > Snapshots and rollback
chunks.text:
It is best-effort by design. On a non-btrfs root, or on a machine where the
snapper `root` config is missing, `ryoku update` proceeds without a snapshot
rather than refusing to update. `ryoku doctor` runs inside every update and,
on a btrfs root with the `root` config missing, creates the config from the
same template the installer uses, registers it in `/etc/conf.d/snapper`,
fixes `/.snapshots` ownership, and enables the cleanup timer, so a drifted
or partially installed machine self-heals on the next run. On a non-btrfs
root, snapshots stay unavailable.

To see what you have:

```bash
ryoku status
ryoku snapshots
```

`ryoku status` prints the snapshot count; `ryoku snapshots` lists them, and
fails clearly when snapper is not configured. If it prints `The config 'root'
does not exist`, see Troubleshoot for the exact
recovery path.

chunks.title: Updates > Snapshots and rollback
chunks.text:
To roll back, pass an id; with no id, `ryoku rollback` lists them so you can
pick one. The same snapshots are selectable from the Limine boot menu when
`limine-snapper-sync` is installed and snapshots exist, so a truly broken
system can be recovered from the bootloader.

```bash
ryoku rollback
ryoku rollback 42
```

This hands off to `sudo snapper rollback`.

chunks.title: Updates > State the CLI keeps
chunks.text:
The CLI keeps its state under `~/.local/state/ryoku/`: the `materialized`
manifest of Ryoku-owned files, the `provisioned` ledger of apps delivered or
left out, and the latest `doctor-report.txt`. During a run it publishes live
progress to `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/ryoku-update.json` for the bar's update island.
See CLI for the full list.

chunks.title: Updates > Status
chunks.text:
`ryoku status` is read-only. It prints the active config base, the installed
`ryoku-desktop` version, what the `[ryoku]` repo offers, the count of pending
package updates (via `checkupdates` from `pacman-contrib`), and the snapshot
count.

```bash
ryoku status
```

The `--json` form is the data seam the Hub and the update island read; it is
not meant for humans.

chunks.title: Updates > Two lanes
chunks.text:
Lane | Command | What moves
**Ryoku** | `ryoku update` | Ryoku's packages from its signed repository, then config and doctor
**Your distribution** | `sudo pacman -Syu` (Arch, CachyOS), `sudo xbps-install -Syu` (Void), `sudo dnf5 upgrade --refresh` (Fedora) | the base system and its kernel

`ryoku update` never moves the kernel or the distribution base on its own: a
Ryoku release stays reversible, and a box that cannot take a distribution
upgrade today can still take a Ryoku fix. Every run reports how many
distribution packages are waiting, and the Updates page lists them.
`ryoku update --system` runs both lanes under one snapshot pair when you want
that; on Void it is the way to keep base updates covered by snapshots.

chunks.title: Updates > What `ryoku update` does
chunks.text:
1. Take a snapper pre-snapshot (best-effort; an unconfigured snapper never
   blocks the update).
2. Upgrade the installed Ryoku packages from the signed Ryoku repository.
3. `ryoku materialize` to re-lay Ryoku's base config under `~/.config`. Your own
   edits live in `~/.config/ryoku/user_edits` and survive every update.
4. `ryoku doctor` to reconcile stateful drift. It also installs, once, an app
   Ryoku now ships by default that this box has never had; an app you removed
   stays removed.
5. Reload the shell.
6. Take a snapper post-snapshot.

Throughout, progress is published to `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/ryoku-update.json`,
which the shell's update island reads to show the run in the bar.

```bash
ryoku update
```

chunks.title: Updates > Where the packages come from
chunks.text:
The desktop ships as signed packages from the Ryoku repository for each
edition: pacman on Arch and CachyOS, XBPS on Void, RPM on Fedora.
`ryoku-desktop` is the umbrella package; the installer adds the repository,
imports the release key, installs `ryoku-desktop` and the variant for your
window manager, and from then on `ryoku update` keeps the machine current.
Apps you left out at install time are recorded and never added back.

Because every Ryoku package is signed and verified on install, an update only
ever applies packages from the real release key. See
Security for how to verify releases yourself.

chunks.title: What's new in 1.0 > Apps
chunks.text:
- RyoManager is the new system monitor and task manager. It is installed by
  default on every edition, can be removed, and reaches existing installs once
  through the doctor without coming back after a removal.
- Kit (`Super + K`) puts the keybinds, every Ryoku command, your phone, dev
  tools and a typing test behind one search field.
- Rashin has two modes: Ask (`Alt + Space`) for quick answers and Agent for
  longer work, plus the Rashin window (`Super + Alt + Space`).
- Redux dictation. On Arch, CachyOS and Fedora the Dictation page in
  Ryoku Settings offers Redux, a fast model for 25 European languages.
  Picking it builds its speech runtime on your machine (it needs git, cmake, a
  C++ compiler and make), and the model card shows each step and the progress.
  Contributed by Sipper1236.

chunks.title: What's new in 1.0 > Desktop
chunks.text:
- Bar styles. A fresh install shows QS Bar. Orpheus, Sumi, Kairos, Shima,
  Python and Nomarchy are the others, and each reads the desktop through the
  same window-manager seam on Hyprland and niri.
- Desktop sounds can be tuned, swapped for your own files or switched off
  in Ryoku Settings > General > Sounds.
- Icon themes are picked in Ryoku Settings > General and apply to GTK,

- The launcher lists Neovim once. The neovim package's own entry used to

The welcome window walks through the keys that open almost everything, Default

The Arch ISO and the script

This page covers what changed since these docs were last refreshed for beta 18
in early September 2026. The per-tree changelogs in the

chunks.title: The QS Bar and the dock > Opening the settings panel
chunks.text:
The bar and the dock have their own GUI, QS Bar Settings, not a Ryoku Hub
page; name it when a user asks how to change the bar from the desktop.

`ryoku-shell bar settings [route]` raises QS Bar Settings on the active
monitor (routes: `bars`, `layout`, `widgets`, `dock`, `community`). It is the
same panel the bar's launcher mark opens; Escape closes it. Layout lists the
three lanes side by side; a move there and a `bar move` from a terminal reach
the same `qsbar.layout`. Community lists every installed bar plugin that is not
Ryoku's own (a manifest without `"official": true`), with its author and a
REMOVE action; a plugin you write for the user lands there.

chunks.title: The QS Bar and the dock > Overview
chunks.text:
The default Ryoku bar is QS Bar (`qsbar`), a full-colour top bar. It is data,
not code: its layout lives in `~/.config/ryoku/shell.json` under `qsbar.layout`,
and every built-in widget and every installed plugin is an entry in the same
list. Drive it with `ryoku-shell bar ...`; the shell daemon is the only writer of
`shell.json`, so never hand-edit the layout.

(The other style, Sumi, is the monochrome frame rail; it has its own frame-bar
model and is not covered here. `barStyle` in `shell.json` picks the style.)

chunks.title: The QS Bar and the dock > The bar CLI
chunks.text:
Every verb goes through the daemon's settings store; a bad id, key, or value is
an error (`err bar: `), never a silent write.

```
bar list [--json]                 every widget: id, label, kind, section, index, shown
bar catalog [--json]              built-ins and installed bar-capable plugins, with settings
bar move  --section  [--index N | --before  | --after ]
bar show  | bar hide      toggle visibility, keeping placement
bar set           a catalogue setting (built-in) or a manifest setting (plugin)
bar position top|bottom
bar form full|fit|dock|notch|islands
bar defaults                      shipped layout and visibility; presentation keys untouched
bar settings [route]              open QS Bar Settings on the active monitor
```

`--json` shapes:

chunks.title: The QS Bar and the dock > The bar CLI
chunks.text:
- `bar list --json`: `[{"id","label","kind","section","index","shown"}]`, where
  `kind` is `"builtin"` or `"plugin"` and `section` is `left|center|right`.
- `bar catalog --json`: the merged catalogue, `{"id","label","gloss","category",
  "desc","kind","settings":[...],"pluginDir"}` per widget, plus `{"hosts":[...]}`
  for plugins.

Examples:

```bash
ryoku-shell bar move clock --section right --index 0
ryoku-shell bar hide gpu
ryoku-shell bar set cputemp barTemperatureSource gpu

chunks.title: The QS Bar and the dock > The layout model
The QS Bar and the dock > The layout model
chunks.text: - An entry is a widget id: a built-in from the catalogue, or an installed plugin's manifest id. Order within a section is the order on the bar. - Placement and visibility are separate. `qsbar.layout` holds only order and section. Whether a built-in renders is `qsbar.widgets[]` (a widget with no visibility key is always shown). A plugin renders when `~/.config/ryoku/plugins.json` has it `enabled` with `host: "topbarGlyph"`. `ryoku-shell bar list` reports both as one `shown` flag, so you never have to know which store answers. - Every id appears at most once. A known widget missing from the layout is appended to `right` (or to its manifest's `defaults.bar.section`). Duplicates are dropped. - Presentation keys keep their own homes and are not placement: `qsbar.barSeps` (separators), `qsbar.iconOnlyGids` (density), `qsbar.widgetColorStyles` (per-widget colour), and the bar-shell keys

chunks.title: The Ryoku GUI map > A worked answer
chunks.text:
The user asks: "how do I make the screen lock after ten minutes?" The GUI-first
answer names the page first:

Open Ryoku Hub with Super+comma and go to Graphics & Power > Idle, or jump
straight there with `ryoku-shell hub open gpu`, then set the lock timer to ten
minutes.

When the user asks YOU to set it, drive the idle daemon directly
(`ryoku-power idle set ac.lockSec 600`, then `ryoku-idle apply`), then tell them
it now locks after ten minutes and that Graphics & Power > Idle is where they see
or change it. Same shape for wallpaper: point them at Super+W first; when you set
it yourself, use `ryogami wallpaper set ` and tell them the picker is
Super+W.

chunks.title: The Ryoku GUI map > Compositor-gated pages
chunks.text:
The Hub shows no page for a capability the running compositor lacks. It gates
Displays (`monitorConfig`), Plugins (`plugins`), Window Manager (a backing
provider), and Layer Rules (shown only with rules present); each appears only
when the active compositor supports it. Animations and the performance and gaming
scripts are Hyprland-specific and do nothing under another compositor. Keybinds
is the deliberate exception: it is compositor-specific yet stays a top-level page
rather than sitting in the compositor group. A setting you change for a
compositor applies only after switching to that compositor.

chunks.title: The Ryoku GUI map > Opening the Hub
chunks.text:
Ryoku Hub is the settings app; it replaces the old reference settings window.
Super+comma opens it. To jump straight to a page, deep-link it by its section
key:

```bash
ryoku-shell hub open              # the Hub, last page
ryoku-shell hub open keybinds     # straight to Keybinds
ryoku-shell hub open gpu          # Graphics & Power
```

The keys are the ones in the table below; they are the same strings the Hub's
rail uses, so `ryoku-shell hub open ` and clicking the rail reach the same
page. Escape closes the Hub.

chunks.title: The Ryoku GUI map > Overview
chunks.text:
Ryoku has a GUI for almost every setting: the Ryoku Hub for system and shell
config, the wallpaper picker for looks, and QS Bar Settings for the bar and the
dock. When a user asks how to change something, name the surface first, then give
the command the page wraps (SKILL.md, "Answer policy: GUI first"). This file is
the lookup from an intent to its surface, its keybind, and the command behind it.

chunks.text:

Change wallpaper or theme | Wallpaper picker | Super+W | `ryogami wallpaper ui` (picker), `ryogami wallpaper set|next|random`

chunks.title: Shell plugins > A worked example
chunks.text:
The user asks: "make me a bar widget that shows my VPN status." The exact
commands:

```bash
ryoku plugin new vpn --bar --name "VPN" --author "Nero "

chunks.title: Shell plugins > content/Panel.qml, manifest.json, README.md; capture the preview png
chunks.text:
ryoku plugin validate ~/Documents/ryoku-plugins/vpn
ryoku plugin add ~/Documents/ryoku-plugins/vpn --bar --yes
```

Then tell the user it is on the bar and under QS Bar Settings > Community, and
stop. Do not run `ryoku plugin share vpn` unless they ask to publish. The VPN
plugin already in Ryostore is the reference safe bar plugin: a glyph that only
reads state, a panel that acts on an explicit click, `pkexec` declared in
`capabilities.privileged`, and `login.tailscale.com` declared in
`capabilities.network`.

chunks.title: Shell plugins > Never share unless asked
chunks.text:
`ryoku plugin share ` opens a public pull request against Ryostore. Do not
run it unless the user explicitly asks to publish. Scaffolding, editing,
validating, and `ryoku plugin add`ing a widget onto the user's own bar is the
whole job; sharing is a separate, opt-in step.

chunks.title: Shell plugins > Overview
chunks.text:
A plugin is a small widget a user drops into the desktop. You write the logic and
the views; Ryoku owns how it looks, moves, sizes, and where it lives, so a plugin
always reads as a native part of the shell. When a user asks you to build a
widget, follow the rules, then run the commands in order. Ryoku never runs a
plugin's code to install it.

chunks.title: Shell plugins > Ryostore
chunks.text:
Ryostore is the curated distribution front for plugins, bar styles, and rices;
community plugins (not `"official": true`) list under a warning that Ryoku does
not review or maintain them. Git and a local folder remain the open door for
anything not in the store. `ryoku plugin share ` is how a widget made here
gets listed there. See `docs/plugins.md` in the Ryoku source for the full
authoring contract.

chunks.title: Shell plugins > Security: the validator's rules
chunks.text:
Blocking (exit 1; `add` refuses without `--allow-findings`): `symlink`,
`escalation` (sudo/doas/su, or pkexec not in `capabilities.privileged`),
`pipe-shell`, `internal-import` (R4), `config-write` (shell.json / plugins.json /
~/.ssh / /etc / rc files), `secret`, `binary`. Warnings (printed, exit 0):
`undeclared-command`, `undeclared-host`, `dynamic-shell` (R9), `outside-write`
(R8), `large-tree` (> 20 MB). `--allow ` downgrades one blocking rule to a
warning for the run.

chunks.title: Shell plugins > Settings types
chunks.text:
Declare user options as a `metadata.settings` schema; the bar renders native
controls and persists changes to `~/.config/ryoku/plugins.json`. Each entry has a
`key`, `type`, `label`, `group`, and `default`. The types the bar renders:

- `toggle` - a boolean switch.
- `choice` - one of a set; give `options: [{ "value", "label" }, ...]`.
- `multi` - several of a set; same `options`.
- `int` - a stepper; give `min` and `max`.
- `text` - a line of text; optional `placeholder`.

`slider` and `image` are desktop-widget menu types and do not render on the bar,
so a bar widget picks from the five above. Read a value guarded, e.g.
`pluginApi.pluginSettings.poll ?? 10`, and write it only through
`pluginApi.saveSetting`.

chunks.title: Shell plugins > The commands, in order
chunks.text:
```
ryoku plugin new  [--bar|--desktop|--popout] [--name N] [--author "N "] [--to ]
ryoku plugin validate  [--json] [--allow ,...]
ryoku plugin add  --bar --yes
ryoku plugin share
```

chunks.title: Shell plugins > The commands, in order
chunks.text: 1. Scaffold. `ryoku plugin new ` writes R1's folder from a working template. `--bar` is the default and also adds `entryPoints.panel` and `content/Panel.qml`. It writes the manifest, `service/Main.qml`, `content/Widget.qml`, `README.md`, `LICENSE`, an `AGENTS.md` with these rules, and a first git commit as the author. 2. Edit. Fill in `service/Main.qml`, `content/Widget.qml`, `content/Panel.qml`, `manifest.json`, and `README.md`; capture `assets/preview-widget.png`. 3. Validate. `ryoku plugin validate ` runs the manifest checks and the static audit, printing `rule-id path:line message`. Clear every blocking finding (see Security). The template validates clean. 4. Install. `ryoku plugin add --bar --yes` validates again, installs through Ryostore's transaction, and enables it on the bar; the shell picks it up on the `plugins.json` change, no restart. `add` refuses blocking findings unless

chunks.title: Shell plugins > The commands, in order
chunks.text:
you pass `--allow-findings`. 5. Verify. Confirm it on the bar and under QS Bar Settings > Community. 6. Share. `ryoku plugin share ` opens the Ryostore pull request. Run it only when the user asks to publish (see below).

Other commands: `ryoku plugin list [--json]` (installed plugins and their host /
enabled state; `--json` rows carry `capabilities`), `ryoku plugin remove `
(uninstall and drop placement), `ryoku plugin export  [--to ]` (a
Ryostore-shaped folder under git).

chunks.title: Shell plugins > The rules
chunks.text:
`ryoku plugin new` writes these into the plugin's `AGENTS.md`;
`ryoku plugin validate` enforces the machine-checkable ones. Follow all eleven.

chunks.title: Shell plugins > The rules
chunks.text: - R1 Place. One folder named after the id, authored under `$(xdg-user-dir DOCUMENTS)/ryoku-plugins//` (fallback `~/ryoku-plugins//`); `ryoku plugin new ` creates it there. Never write into `~/.local/share/ryoku/plugins/` or `~/.config/quickshell/`. - R2 Shape. `manifest.json` at the root; `service/Main.qml` (logic, no UI); `content/Widget.qml`; optional `content/Panel.qml`; `README.md`; `LICENSE`; `assets/preview-widget.png` (a real capture); scripts only under `bin/` with a shebang and the exec bit. List every extra file in manifest `files`. - R3 Id. Lowercase `a-z0-9*`, unique, not a built-in widget id. - R4 Imports. Only `QtQuick*`, `Quickshell*`, `Ryoku.PluginKit`, `Ryoku.PluginKit.Singletons`, and files inside the plugin folder. Never `shell.*`, `Ryoku.Ui*` internals, or a relative import that climbs out. - R5 Settings. Declared in `metadata.settings`; read through

chunks.title: Shell plugins > The rules
chunks.text: `pluginApi.pluginSettings` behind a default; written only through `pluginApi.saveSetting(key, value)`. Never edit `shell.json` or `plugins.json`. - R6 Commands. Every external program is in the plugin's own `bin/` or listed in `dependencies.commands`. No `sudo`, `doas`, `su`. Escalate only through `pkexec`, only on an explicit click, only when listed in `capabilities.privileged` (exact command strings) and explained in the README. - R7 Network. Every host is listed in `capabilities.network`. No `curl … | sh`, no downloading and running code. - R8 Files. Write only under `pluginApi.stateDir` (`$XDG_STATE_HOME/ryoku/plugins/`), `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/ryoku/plugins/`, or a temp dir. Never touch `~/.ssh`, `/etc`, shell rc files, or another plugin's folder. - R9 Shell. No `sh -c` with a string built from settings or program output; pass argv arrays. - R10 Secrets and binaries. No tokens, keys or

chunks.title: Shell plugins > The rules
chunks.text: credentials in the tree; no compiled binaries (ELF/Mach-O/`.so`) and no symlinks; scripts only. - R11 Honesty. `official` is never `true` for a community plugin; `author` is `Name `; the README states what runs, reads, writes, and every privileged or network capability.

chunks.title: Shell plugins > What a plugin ships
chunks.text:
```
/
  manifest.json        what it is, its hosts, its defaults, and its settings schema
  service/Main.qml     persistent logic and state, no UI
  content/Widget.qml   the one view, rendered at the host's density
  content/Panel.qml    optional: a bar plugin's panel (opens under the glyph)
  bin/                 optional scripts (shebang + exec bit)
  README.md            what it runs, reads, writes, and every capability
  LICENSE
  assets/preview-widget.png
```

Installed plugins live at `~/.local/share/ryoku/plugins//` (receipt-owned;
never author there). The three hosts are `topbarGlyph` (a mark on the QS Bar),
`desktopWidget` (a tile on the wallpaper), and `framePopout` (a surface that
grows from a screen edge, or floats centred).

chunks.title: Shell plugins > What the host sets
chunks.text:
Declare these on your roots and read them; never assign them.

`content/Widget.qml` on the bar (host `topbarGlyph`):

Property | Value
`density` | `"glyph"`
`widthBudget` | `220` (cap any text you draw to it)
`s` | scale multiplier; multiply sizes and font sizes by it
`active` | `true` while mounted
`screen` | the monitor this copy is on
`pluginApi` | your handle (below)

`content/Panel.qml` (a bar plugin's panel, `entryPoints.panel`):

Property | Value
`density` | `"full"`
`widthBudget` | manifest `panel.width` (default `320`, clamped `240..520`)
`s` | scale multiplier
`active` | `true` while the panel is open
`pluginApi` | your handle (below)

The panel reports its `implicitHeight`; the host sizes the card to it, capped to
the screen. Widget.qml's left click opens it: `onClicked: pluginApi.togglePanel()`.
No click on the bar ever mutates anything.

chunks.title: Shell plugins > What the host sets
chunks.text:
The `pluginApi` every entry point receives:

Member | What it is
`mainInstance` | your live `service/Main.qml` instance
`pluginSettings` | the resolved settings; read each key behind its default
`pluginDir` | the installed plugin folder (build `bin/` paths from it)
`stateDir` | `$XDG_STATE_HOME/ryoku/plugins/`; the only place you write (R8)
`saveSetting(key, value)` | persist one setting; `pluginSettings` re-derives (R5)
`panelOpen` / `openPanel()` / `closePanel()` / `togglePanel()` | the bar panel
